speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: EXPRESSION OF GOOD WISHES ON BECOMING SOVEREIGN STATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the house is aware the Belgian Congo is to become a sovereign state today, and all members of the house will wish to join in extending best wishes to this new country on joining the family of independent nations. In keeping with the Congo's new status I wish to announce that the Canadian trade commissioner's office, which has been for some years maintained at Leopoldville, is to become a full consulate general. The change in status will constitute tangible evidence to the Congolese of Canada's interest in the future of their new state, and it will lend additional importance to commercial contacts with the new government.

Can the minister indicate the possibilities of the herring industry on the west coast coming under this act?

The fisheries prices support board have, I think, had this question under review. Many difficulties are involved. One is, as I said yesterday, that there is the very grave danger of countervailing duties on subsidized products. The position is such that Canada exports a very high percentage of her production of fish meal and fish oil. Our markets are found in countries which also produce fish meal, although not enough for their own purposes; therefore they import some. The result is that the situation is very sensitive to anything that might be considered to be undercutting home production as far as those chief markets of ours are concerned, namely European countries and the United States.

Because herring are used primarily for the production of meal and oil, has any thought been given to the reconstitution of the industry to the point where it may be able to engage in the production of herring for food consumption purposes? What snags have we run into in that regard?

In other words it is a question of an economic market for the product. Certain types of herring are produced in small quantities as a luxury food, but this is only a relatively small percentage of the total potential supply and would only support a very small segment of the herring fishing industry. In order to have any real impact on the industry you would have to have a very large market for herring to be used as food, and there appears to be none in sight that would allow the industry to operate on an appreciably large scale in an economic way.
I am sorry I was not here during the full time this matter was discussed yesterday. Do soybeans have any detrimental competitive effect upon the herring meal and oil industry?

Yes. As a matter of fact all fish meals are used chiefly as a supplement for animal feeds because of their high protein content. There are many alternative sources for various types of proteins, and there are only a few types of animal feeds in which fish meal is desirable at a relatively high price. I am not an authority on this matter, but I understand that such feeds as chick starter would be an example where there is a greater desire to use fish

meal than is the case with other types of animal feeds. With respect to most types of animal feeds, if fish meal is at a high price the mixer of the animal feed can substitute other protein sources.

I am afraid that as one accepts responsibility one finds that life can be very complicated as far as the administration of a country is concerned, where you have such a divergent group of interests. The situation with regard to soybeans is different because of the fact that they are largely marketed in Canada and we do not export them to any extent. Their use as a substitute for fish meal is not their only use. As a matter of fact, soybean oil is used for many commercial purposes as well as food purposes.
The minister has just indicated the great necessity in this country of applying a little socialist philosophy and planning so that we would not get into these difficulties.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think it has not been customary for ministers of justice to make any statement on the first item, departmental administration, but rather to answer any questions that might be raised with regard to the administration of the department. I propose to follow that course. However, if it will be of assistance to hon. members who wish to discuss specific matters I propose to make a short statement when we reach item 161, having to do with the administration of the office of the commissioner of penitentiaries. I expect to be making a sort of brief progress report on correctional reform.

First of all, in opening the discussion on the estimates of the Department of Justice, I should like to pay our respects and to offer our compliments to both Mr. Jackett and Mr. Favreau who we know are to leave the department. As far as I know, while they were there they did a magnificent job and discharged their duties in an able manner. We on this side of the chamber want to wish them well as they enter upon their new activities. We are sure they will have in their private practice of law as much success as they had when they were senior officials of the Department of Justice.
There is one matter to which I should now like to come, and my remarks are prompted by a discussion that was held in this chamber on Monday. I refer to a question that was asked by my friend the hon. member for Vancouver East of the Minister of Justice, namely whether the necessity to increase the number of judges in the superior court in the province of Quebec was owing to the increase in criminality in that province. I am now referring to page 5654 of the French

text of Hansard of Monday last, and I quote the Minister of Justice in French:
(Translation):
In reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Vancouver East, I regret that even with the best will in the world I cannot give a categorical answer as to why there is this fairly steady pressure for an increase in the number of judges; whether it is simply because of the increase in population or because of the increase in population accompanied by an increase in criminality.
A little further on, the minister added this:
With respect to the question, or that aspect of it dealing with criminality, the best assessment that I have been able to make is that there is not an absolute increase in criminality but that there is a proportionate increase, an increase in keeping with the increase in population, yes, and also with the increased trend toward urbanization. (Text):
Inasmuch as the population of Canada is increasing, Mr. Chairman, there is no doubt that criminality is increasing; but that surely was not the factor accounting for the increase in the number of judges in the province of Quebec. I want to say right away that I do not think for one moment that my friend the hon. member for Vancouver East was of the opinion that criminality was worse in Quebec than anywhere else in Canada, and I am sure that thought did not enter the mind of the Minister of Justice. However, I should like to make a few remarks on that matter and show that the increase in the number of judges in Quebec was necessitated by several other factors.
It might be useful to explain generally how the courts function in Quebec, inasmuch as possibly they are not functioning in the same way as are courts in some other provinces, because the judges do not have the same functions or the same jurisdiction. First the accused are brought before a justice of the peace, a magistrate or a justice of the court of sessions of the peace. There, of course, they have a preliminary inquiry when such an inquiry is indicated, or they have their trial before the judge sitting in what we usually call the court below. The main criminal cases in the province of Quebec are tried and decided before those courts. As is the situation anywhere else in Canada, only the major crimes come before the assizes. I know for a fact that in the district of Montreal the criminal assizes are presided over by a justice of the superior court, and more often than not it is Mr. Justice Lazure, who sits in assize four times a year. Every sitting extends for a month or a month and a half. So there is only one judge in Montreal occupied by criminal courts.
In Quebec city there are normally two terms of assizes, and even there they occupy only one judge. In what I might call the 79951-0-353J
Supply-Justice
rural districts around Montreal and Quebec city there is only one term of assizes every year, normally in October. I know the old district of which I was a member, the district of Arthabaska, had two years in a row when there was no assize at all. In my own district, which was formed in 1956, there has not been one since that time, which perhaps speaks well for the honesty of the people in my riding.
The main reason for this recommendation for an increase in the number of judges is not due to criminality at all. If my memory serves me well, in 1867 there were 33 judges of the superior court in the province of Quebec. Now, as the result of legislation which was passed last Monday, there are 55, not quite twice as many. The population in 1867 was less than one million but now it is over five million. So there is no doubt that the more population there is in any province or in the whole country the more court sittings there are.
The judges of the superior court in Quebec deal mostly with civil litigation. The number of cases has increased tremendously. In my own district in 1956 there were over 160 cases on the roll at the beginning of the term and the judge sits only once a month over nine months. So there is no doubt that there cases are dragging on, and it takes at least two years to have a case heard by the court after inscription on the roll.
Those cases are not necessarily dealing with property or personal damages; it is mostly litigation concerning automobile accidents. According to statistics, although I have not the figures before me, at least half the cases tried before the superior courts in the province of Quebec arose from automobile accidents, and this might be the case in some of the other provinces too. Those cases take up half the time of the judges. The rest of the cases are the ordinary sort arising from the increase in population, the increase in business and especially the increase in book debts. The more we grow the more we have to sue people because they do not pay their debts. One or other of the opposing lawyers often seeks a delay, but these cases are apt to come before the courts and they do occupy the time of the judges.
Mr. Chairman, those are the preliminary remarks I wanted to make on this first item. I might have something more to say and some questions to ask as we go along. Before I resume my seat I would like to make a request of the Minister of Justice. One of my colleagues in the official opposition wanted to speak on this first item but is now engaged on some other business. Perhaps this item might stand until he returns, and perhaps we might carry on and return to it later.

I was very pleased to hear the statement by the Minister of Justice that it is his intention when we reach the penitentiary item to make a statement in regard to the penitentiaries. I presume it will relate mostly to the corrective procedures and policies which have been adopted under the new set up of the parole board. I hope when the minister speaks he will not necessarily make his remarks brief; I hope he will take time to go into some detail and outline the situation Canada is facing in the realm of criminology.
In the most recent report of the commissioner of penitentiaries there is some very disturbing and alarming information. According to the report, which covers a period of 12 months, of those who were committed to the penitentiaries in that period of time 82.88 per cent were guilty of general recidivism. So that of the penitentiary committals in the past 12 months, 82.88 per cent had previously been either in a reformatory, in a provincial jail or in a penitentiary.
That in itself gives evidence of a very serious situation, but it is even more alarming because we note from the report that of the committals to the penitentiaries in that 12-month period-

speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member would permit me to suggest that it would be more convenient, I believe to him as well as to me, if his discussion of this problem and of penal problems generally could be deferred till we reach item 161, which is the general item referring to penitentiaries and correctional measures. The staff of the penitentiaries branch are not here; therefore I would not be able to reply to the hon. member as fully as I would want. I expect we will have a discussion of penitentiaries and correctional problems on that item, so I wonder if it would not suit the hon. member's purpose if he deferred his remarks on that aspect of my responsibility until that item is reached.

I understand the statement of the minister in this regard and I quite agree with him, but unfortunately with the meetings of committees and certain other matters there is a possibility that at that particular moment I might not be able to be here. It is for that reason that I make these few remarks on the first item of the minister's estimates in an effort to indicate some of the phases upon which I know many of us would like to hear the minister when we reach the item dealing with penitentiaries.
As I was saying, of the committals to the penitentiaries in this 12-month period, 46.41 per cent have been in the penitentiary before. So they are recidivists with penitentiary experience. I would like to draw the attention of

the committee to this fact, that of the 2,922 persons who were committed as recidivists with penitentiary experience, 1,423 were in the penitentiary for the second time, 760 were in the penitentiary for the third time, 366 for the fourth time, and 373 were back in the penitentiary for the fifth time or more.
Those figures as given to us in the report of the commissioner of penitentiaries indicates the very serious nature of the problem, and I would most certainly like to have as full a statement as possible from the Minister of Justice as to how this problem is being tackled and what is the policy for dealing with it which he has in mind. It is quite obvious that we have a group who are strictly of criminal tendency and who will not learn.
I must admit that I cannot understand why a person who has been in a penitentiary should decide to go back. I am one of the fortunate few who can go to a penitentiary and get out again. I often visit penitentiaries and jails, and I cannot understand why a person who has won his freedom should, by committing some criminal act, render himself liable to go back to that kind of life.
I do want to say how much I appreciate the action of the minister in attempting something new as far as British Columbia is concerned, namely the inauguration of an institution which is to some extent an open prison. I refer to the installation at William Head, and I should like to place on record two quotations from the report of the commissioner dealing with that institution because I think they give an indication that the policy which has commended itself to the minister, and which he is endeavouring to extend, may be at least a partial answer to the problem I have outlined. I note that on page 130 of the report the commissioner has this to say:
The William Head installation is an innovation, and the consensus of opinion to date is that it has been an unqualified success. The open type installation tends to release the tension in the better type of inmate, and the ones selected for transfer to William Head have the feeling that they are trusted, and up to the present time this trust has not been misplaced. The fact that there are no walls or bars on the windows adds to the inmate's feeling of confidence and feeling that the administration have confidence in him makes him more confident in himself when he is released.
Again, on page 131, we find the following statement still in relation to the William Head installation:
Many such transfers have taken place without untoward incident. These achievements indicate that inmates do respond to humane, considerate treatment on the part of the authorities, and it is possible to maintain firm discipline without arousing the animosity of the individual, thus taking a long step towards successful reformation and rehabilitation.

We are very pleased to note that this has been the experience and that this is the view of the authorities in charge of this experiment, if such it is. Should this be the consensus we hope there may be a statement forthcoming from the Minister of Justice as to the extension of this system, not only on the basis of the present installation at William Head but also-I think there is one at Collins Bay-

Oh, yes; that is the one that is going to be opened this fall, at Springhill. We do hope such institutions as these may help to provide a solution to this very serious problem of recidivism.
May I add that one of the reasons we have this general recidivism is in my opinion because we have failed so far to pay sufficient attention to after-care services. It is significant, I think, that so far this year the money we have expended on such organizations as are named in the report has amounted to only $60,000. That, it seems to me, is a remarkably small sum in the light of the seriousness of this problem.
It will not do to anticipate that as soon as a person is discharged from prison he will, as a result of the work done by the training instructors, the ministers, the doctors, the psychiatrists and the psychologists, be able to walk out of a penitentiary having the desired social conscience. Society must follow up the effort which has been made. It must take an interest in where these people go, whom they resort with and whether or not they can find employment. It is difficult enough at the present time for people who possess a social conscience and who live by the law to obtain employment. It is far more difficult for a person who has broken the law to do so.
I have found out in discussions with many who have come out of prison, and many who have gone back, that because of their weakness they gave way to temptation when after a few weeks, or a month or so, they were unable to obtain employment. The very small amount, the picayune amount, of help which they are able to get from organizations which assist prisoners after their discharge is certainly not adequate. This is particularly true with regard to the problem of those who have been incarcerated as a result of drug addiction. Greater emphasis must be placed on after care service and the following up of cases in the period after discharge.
I hope the minister will devote great attention to following up the cases of those who are discharged from our penitentiaries and seeing that they are given every assistance
Supply-Justice
possible in rehabilitating themselves. In my opinion it is foolish to spend the large sums of money which are required to maintain people in our jails and penitentiaries, not only to punish them but also to try to rehabilitate them, and then, for a matter of dollars, leave them on their own with the result that we are faced with these figures demonstrating such a high degree of recidivism. If no other plan is forthcoming I hope the minister will seriously consider a system under which they could at least draw unemployment insurance so as to help them keep on the straight and narrow path. Any money spent after sentence has been completed to keep these people in line as socially conscious individuals is money well invested and will undoubtedly save a great deal more to the taxpayers of the country in the long run.
That is all I have to say on this subject at the moment. I do hope the minister will also take note of one or two other questions, and perhaps comment on them when he replies. I understand that the Department of Justice and the Department of Health and Welfare have been working sincerely and conscientiously to evolve some approach to this problem of drug addiction. It is my understanding that these studies have practically reached a conclusion, and that the minister himself regrets it is not possible for him to introduce at this session certain changes he may have in mind, because of the necessity of receiving the complete co-operation of the provincial authorities. However, I hope the minister can at least give us some indication of the nature of his new approach to the question of drug addiction, both in terms of care and of punishment should that be necessary.
There can be no question at all but that we are going to continue to be faced with this problem in Canada until we do recognize drug addiction as an illness, as something that has to be treated; and we are not going to solve it by treating drug addicts strictly as criminals. I know the minister appreciates the problem we have in Canada and particularly in British Columbia. All the reports that I have received seem to indicate that we have somewhere in the neighbourhood of between 1,500 and 2,000 drug addicts in the city of Vancouver alone. The minimum figure I have ever noticed is 1,500.
From my study of this and from the reports of those who have made a lifetime study of it -and their recent conclusions indicate this- a drug addict has to have at least three capsules of heroin a day. According to the latest figures I have received from unofficial sources, a capsule of heroin costs $5 on the Vancouver market, and sometimes $7 or $9. Therefore a drug addict requires a minimum of $15 a day

Supply-Justice
for three capsules. If we have 1,500 addicts in Vancouver we have some indication of the money being spent. Since the majority of those who are drug addicts are not of the wealthy class, it is almost axiomatic that they must resort to criminal activity to obtain the money necessary to buy the drugs.
Therefore we have the problem of the addicts resorting to crime, since they must obtain a great deal of money if they are to get sufficient to buy the necessary capsules. So the question of treatment is most important. I have ideas on this, and I have mentioned them almost every time I have spoken on this subject in the house. I am not going to repeat them now, because the minister is well aware of them and because representations on this subject were made to the Senate committee when they held their meetings in the city of Vancouver. I do hope the minister has been successful in evolving a plan of such a nature that he feels fairly confident it is one in which he can get the necessary co-operation from the provincial governments in order that as soon as possible a great step forward can be made in handling this problem of drug addiction.
There is another point I should like to bring to the attention of the minister before I sit down and ask him whether it is possible to do anything about it. Over the recent weeks in particular I have been receiving complaints about the operations of so-called collection agencies. These agencies are companies that buy up the bills that are owing to business concerns for anywhere from 10 cents to 50 cents on the dollar; then they go after those who owe them money and, in my opinion, they do it in a most vicious manner and under circumstances which, because the average person is honest and wants to pay his bills, cause a great deal of hardship to those concerned. As a matter of fact they resort to practices in trying to bleed those who have not the money to pay that it almost looks to me as though they are in contempt of the law. Because of the way in which they put out their dunning letters a person who is easily frightened or does not know very much about the law would almost think he was being served with a subpoena. If it is not a subpoena, they certainly think it is some sort of legal paper and that they had better find some way of paying up or they are in real trouble.
I have one file on them. Here is the type of communication that is sent out by the credit bureau of Vancouver. If you look at the paper you will see that it looks like a subpoena right off the bat. If you look at the wording you will realize that it scares people. This is how it reads:

We have now decided to give our solicitor instruction to go ahead with court action against you, but before doing so we write you this final letter to inform you:
"That a judgment is good for 20 years and a warrant of execution may be directed to the sheriff at any time thereafter requiring him to make a seizure to satisfy the claim and all costs. A judgment debtor can be made to appear before the court for examination, and garnisheeing proceedings can be taken either before or after judgment attaching moneys in the bank, salary or wages, and moneys due from other source."
We are allowing you another three days to think it over. Please bear in mind we do not want to have this summons served. We would much rather give you a receipt.
I think after all these years I know a little bit about law and procedure, but I did not know before that a judgment is good for 20 years and that a warrant of execution may be directed to the sheriff at any time thereafter requiring him to make a seizure, garnisheeing wages, taking goods and everything else. I say this is going too far and that some kind of control should be exercised over collection agencies. I am not certain whether this comes within the legislative jurisdiction of the federal government or whether it is something that has to be handled wholly and solely on the basis of provincial jurisdiction.
I did want to draw this to the attention of the minister. It is a most serious matter right today for many thousands of people in Canada, and I know it has affected a great many people in British Columbia and particularly in the city of Vancouver. I hope the Minister of Justice can make some comment on this and state whether it is possible for federal legislative action to be taken to control these people, or whether his department can exercise any sort of inspection over their actions.
These are three of the matters that I wanted to draw to the attention of the minister under the first item. I hope my duties on committees will not make it necessary for me to be absent when the minister gives details on other items. I know the interest of the minister in penitentiaries and in the problems of my colleagues. It will mean a great deal to this country and to all of us in this committee if at this time, when his estimates are going through, the minister can give us information that will mark a real advance forward in the handling of those problems.

Mr. Chairman, I also wish to say a few words about the problem of drug addiction. I do so for two reasons. First, out of some 3,400 addicts in Canada, half are found in British Columbia and more particularly in the city of Vancouver, and most of their activities appear to centre around a certain area in my riding of Vancouver Centre.

Second, Mr. Chairman, there appears to be a growing number of juvenile addicts. In 1957, for example, there were 25 teenagers in Canada who were drug addicts. In 1958 there were 47, and in 1959 the number had increased to 55. Of the 55, 17 were males and 38 were females. British Columbia has the dubious distinction of having the majority of those teenagers, because of the figure of 17 males and 38 females, 15 of the males and 31 of the females are to be found in that province.
While I am concerned with the drug problem as it affects all addicts, I feel a special sense of responsibility toward those teenagers who are addicts. The over-all number of addicts in Canada does not show any marked increase, whereas the number of addicts who are teenagers has indicated a rise. The over-all figures show the following numbers in the years 1954 to 1959 inclusive:
Year	Number
1954		 3,212
1955		 3,425
1956		 3,421
1957		 3,315
1958		 3,412
1959		 3,408
It would therefore appear that apart from teenage addicts there is some tendency toward stabilization in the number of addicts.
Prior to speaking on this subject I was faced with the problem of trying to justify in my own mind whatever sums of money the government intends to spend in advancing and implementing a program of treatment for addicts. I also had to learn something about the narcotic problem. Therefore during the Easter recess this year I visited Oakalla prison farm at Vancouver where I interviewed male and female drug addicts who were serving their sentences there. I spoke to the senior prison officials at Oakalla. I had discussions with the director of the narcotic foundation in Vancouver. I spoke to a number of addicts outside of Oakalla, and when I returned to Ottawa I discussed the problem with senior officials of the R.C.M.P. and the Department of National Health and Welfare. I have read the speech on the narcotic problem which the Minister of Justice delivered to the Canadian club in Vancouver on April 20, 1960, and I have also read a number of reports and papers on this subject.
I must admit, Mr. Chairman, that prior to my research I felt that if the government were to spend large sums of money on a comprehensive program to help some 3,000 to 4,000 people, that money might well be spent on a segment of the population which was more numerous and more deserving such as, for example, our old age pensioners. After
Supply-Justice
all, addicts are only a very small part of our population and, far from contributing to society, society instead has to pay for their misdeeds. None the less, after seeing and speaking to addicts I realized that most of them were people in an age group who under normal circumstances would be wage earners engaged in bringing up families and who would therefore be making a useful contribution to society. I accordingly came to the conclusion that we would justify any measure which would help to restore these people to a useful role, because in so helping to rehabilitate these people we would have to come to grips with the more basic problem of crime, namely the reasons for delinquency.
If we do not do anything about the problem of drug addiction we lose not only the contribution which these addicts might have made to society; we also have to bear the loss to the community in terms of actual dollars and cents. As an example of the financial loss to the community, which was mentioned by the previous speaker, let me illustrate the case of an addict who is faced with the problem of gratifying his craving for drugs. Heroin, which is the most popular drug for Canadian addicts, sells for approximately $5 a capsule. It might cost more or less depending on market conditions. The Vancouver Sun on March 26 of this year reported a Vancouver drug squad detective as saying that as the result of a police seizure of 91 ounces of heroin worth $1 million, smalltime peddlers were afraid to go into Vancouver streets for fear of being hijacked by addicts desperate for illegal narcotics. The same detective was quoted as saying that the price of a capsule would go up from $5 when supplies started to flow again, and that as a result of the seizure known addicts were seen wandering the streets and in cafes in a certain area of Vancouver suffering withdrawal symptoms. Incidentally, the person who was found to possess the 91 ounces of heroin was sentenced to serve 14 years.
The usual daily consumption of an addict using heroin runs between five and ten capsules. Female addicts appear to get by on the minimum dosage but male addicts seem to want more and to take all they can get. But basing my calculation on the minimum figures of five capsules, this would cost the addict $25 a day. Very few people can afford this kind of money. Multiplying $25 per day by 1,797, the number of known addicts in Vancouver, we have a figure of $44,925 per day. Addicts do not have steady employment, and even if they did their wages would not be sufficient to fulfil their craving for drugs. So where does the money come from? It comes from petty thievery, from prostitution and other forms of crime.

Supply-Justice
The sum of approximately $45,000 paid out each day for illegal drugs would be bad enough, but it is a known fact that stolen goods which are disposed of through a "fence" generally bring in only a third of their true worth. In order to get $25 an addict would therefore have to steal approximately $75 worth of goods. Multiply $75 by 1,797 again, we get the figure of $134,775 per day.
I would be the first to admit, Mr. Chairman, that these are hypothetical figures. The sums I have mentioned are probably overestimated for a number of reasons, but I did want to impress upon hon. members the potential loss in terms of money. To the figures which I have given must be added the cost of keeping addicts in a penal institution. There is another loss which in my opinion is even greater and which cannot be calculated in terms of dollars and cents. I refer to the break-up of homes and the resulting unhappiness and delinquency which invariably follow such disruption.
What are we going to do about this problem? I know there have been many reports and suggestions, but I was interested to hear from the addicts themselves that they wished to be treated as medical cases and as persons in need of psychiatric treatment rather than to be treated as criminals. After all, they argue, we do not treat alcoholics as criminals unless, of course, they commit a crime while their faculties are impaired, so why should addicts be considered criminals?
Here I wish to clear up a popular misconception, namely that all drug addicts while under the influence of drugs are bent on murder, mayhem or rape. Studies indicate that the users of heroin desire only to enjoy the pleasant effects of their favourite drug in a quiet relaxed and private way. The user is so relaxed while under the influence of heroin that he probably could not punch his way out of a paper bag, and in committing theft in order to get enough money to buy drugs the addict is doing so only because stealing has been a behaviour pattern even before he started to take drugs.
In stating that they wished to be treated as medical cases rather than as criminals, the addicts themselves have expressed to me the desire to be confined in an institution which would enable them to be apart from the usual criminals and where they could aiso receive psychiatric help. Many of the addicts do not themselves understand the true reasons for their addiction, and I was baffled in the beginning by some of the answers 1 received when I asked them why they took drugs. I remember asking one girl if there was anything in her family background which might have contributed to her

desire for drugs, and she replied that she came from a wealthy family; that she had all the material things she wanted, and that she had been one of the debutantes who had been introduced to society at one of the balls held in the hotel Vancouver. She could give no reason except that she liked taking heroin. I asked one of the boys why he took drugs, and he replied that he did so because he found himself the centre of interest for the girls at his school; that by being known as a drug addict he could get a girl any time he wanted.
These answers, among others, indicated to me that drug addiction might be a result and not a cause of delinquency. Most of the reports I have read and the discussions I have had support this view, and that is why I can reconcile the spending of money to help solve this basic aspect of delinquency.
It may be an oversimplification of the situation, but I do think that if we were able to assist in preventing the break-up of families; if we were able to provide more recreational facilities for our young people, and if we were able to help those who are in great financial need, we would be going a long way toward solving the whole crime problem. Granted that every person is responsible for his own behaviour, we still cannot escape the final responsibility of society to those who need help, particularly in our own communities, whether such help be financial, spiritual or moral.
Having made some study of this problem, I was delighted to read the speech which the Minister of Justice delivered on April 20, 1960 to the Canadian club in Vancouver, and in which he presented the attitude of the government toward this problem. Not only is there a sympathetic attitude but there is also in that speech the announcement of a comprehensive plan to deal with this problem. From my reading of the statement of the Minister of Justice dated May 16, 1960 I am gratified to learn that the government is taking active steps to implement, in conjunction with the provincial authorities, a program of prevention and correction.
The plan as outlined by the minister contains many of the suggestions which I received from the addicts with whom I spoke. However, I would urge that both the federal government and the provincial governments give serious thought to providing even more comprehensive psychiatric treatment. This form of treatment is very expensive, but I think it is the key to the whole program of prevention and correction. In Ontario and British Columbia, where most of the addicts are found, it might be possible, notwithstanding the division between

federal and provincial responsibilities, to establish some institutions administered jointly by the two levels of government to achieve this objective of providing treatment centres. Addicts could be sent to these two major centres of treatment, and the pressure on provincial and federal institutions for accommodation might be relieved.
Finally I should like to say a few words about the maximum sentence of 14 years which can be imposed on the trafficker. I know that it is extremely difficult to arrest and convict a key person in an organization formed to distribute illegal drugs but I wonder, Mr. Chairman, if the form of treatment which was used in China at one time for opium addicts might not help to stamp out or at least drastically reduce the number of pushers and traffickers. This treatment consisted of extending clemency on the first and second occasions on which an addict was arrested. He would even be offered free medical treatment on these two occasions, but if he were caught a third time he was simply taken to Peking and placed against the wall of the temple of heaven and shot. I have no direct knowledge of the effectiveness either of the treatment or the mode of treatment, but I think until such a drastic punishment is provided to deter those who would traffic in drugs purely for monetary gain, we shall always have a problem on our hands.
Once again I should like to congratulate the Minister of Justice upon his announced intention of introducing a comprehensive plan to deal with the problem of drug addiction in Canada. With the federal government showing the way, I hope the provincial governments will find it possible to enter into an early agreement with the federal government on those matters which fall under provincial jurisdiction, so that we may get started on a program which has been long overdue.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I intend to make my remarks brief, but before mentioning the two matters I should like to discuss this afternoon I may say that the committee listened with interest to what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre as well as the hon. member for Vancouver East. These are problems which are complex and difficult, and I know that all of us sympathize with the minister and his department in their efforts to find a solution for a matter of this kind.
I rose to deal briefly, as I said, not with a specific matter such as the one to which reference has been made but a matter which is general in its nature. I remember that not so very long ago Bishop Fulton Sheen, in opening one of his telecasts which unfor-
Supply-Justice
tunately are not seen any longer on the C.B.C., had this to say, that crime in the United States has attained alarming proportions. Did you know that every 40 minutes in that country there was a murder; that the crime of rape took place every 30 minutes; that a theft took place every 7 minutes; that armed robbery took place every 1 minute and that at every 2.4 seconds of the day an automobile was stolen? These are indeed revealing statistics. While I do not know what the statistics are for our own country, I presume that on a proportional basis there would be some resemblance to them.
What prompts me to rise now is this. What is there that can be done by those of us who sit in this house, by the Department of Justice and the officers of the department, to remedy a situation which is attaining alarming proportions in the country, particularly in the areas in which there is a concentration of population? Of course the main answer lies in education and in the development and building of character. For that I am sure the minister and this house have no responsibility.
What else can be done? It may be that the minister will be able to enlighten the committee in this respect, and knowing him as I do I am sure he will not deal with this subject other than in an objective way, which is the manner in which I propose to deal with it now. I have no answer to the problem which seems to be aggravating itself and which is not the sole responsibility of a department, let alone a minister. It is the result of a set of circumstances, of the world in which we live and of so many reasons that I would not be living up to the statement I made earlier that I intended to speak briefly if I were to go into all of those reasons.
I think now of the great metropolitan area of Montreal, and I come quickly to what I have in mind.
I wonder whether any consideration has been given by the department to removing to outlying areas a penitentiary which lies in that city. From the information that I have been able to obtain and from conversations I have had with members of the bar and of the judiciary, that factor seems to be perhaps one of the many reasons for the increase in crime. That consideration may apply elsewhere; I do not know. I do not even know that it applies in the city of Montreal. But from judges who sit on cases in the city of Montreal I have been told that when parole is granted to hardened criminals who have been in these institutions they find themselves coming out in the same environment as that in which they found themselves when they were convicted of a former crime; and the

Supply-Justice
temptation is so great that they go on and commit similar offences again. Would it not be advisable and profitable for the state to build these institutions-about which I will have more to say on another vote-outside of these great centres? Perhaps the minister might deem it advisable to say something on that score later on.
The other matter I wanted to bring to his attention was this; and again I am sure he will take it, inasmuch as it is critical, with the good grace with which he generally takes other comments. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police of late have been making statements which in my opinion were not of a police or judicial nature.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I wonder whether I could suggest to my hon. friend that I think it would be more to his interest and to mine if his discussion could be deferred until we reach the first item under the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, at which time I will have the officers of the police here and will be able to reply more fully and directly to what the hon. member may say.

speechtext: I have no objection to doing that, Mr. Chairman. However, I was just going to make one statement and resume my seat. As the minister knows, I have the right to deal with this matter on the first item and I am not going to be lengthy. The only point I was raising was this. Mr. Chairman, last year the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) introduced a resolution in this house for the purpose of defining section 150 of the Criminal Code, dealing with obscene publications. That bill had long been awaited by a great number of Canadians. The Minister of Justice is well acquainted with this problem, since he played an important part in the Senate investigation of 1952-53.
At this stage of my remarks, Mr. Chairman, allow me to quote an excerpt from the August 1959 issue of the publication Relations:
Let us not assume that the new legislation will be a cure-all. It will prove an effective instrument for those judges who are anxious to improve

social environment. This means a great deal. It will be left to them to decide whether the dominant characteristic of an incriminated publication is obscene, whether the author is unduly exploiting violence and sex. Obviously, their education and turn of mind will affect their judgments. So will the general attitude of the people. In this field, more than in any other perhaps, legislation no matter how well conceived, can be effective only with the courageous and continued support of high-minded people. Mr. Fulton is to be commended for his new legislation, and the firm and straightforward support he is getting from all the people.
The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) rightly said a moment ago that a wave of crime is now sweeping over the whole North American continent. This increase is probably due in great part to filthy publications. Therefore, I wish to denounce publicly and strongly certain most objectionable material that is being published, printed, and then distributed by a great many newsstands in the province of Quebec, and surely in some parts of Ontario too. The following list was issued by the national federation of the Holy Name society:
1.	For the peace of their conscience, Christians must not sell, buy or read the following weeklies.
2.	Municipalities must prohibit their sale within their jurisdiction.
3.	Organizations must caution their members against them.
4.	Those weeklies are objectionable because
of their pictures and writings on sex, S;
of their crime stories, C;
of their gossip, G.
As the case may be, they are marked by the signs: *'S" or "C" or "G".
Mr. Chairman, here is the list of those obscene publications, harmful to the morals of young people and of the population:
Alio Police; Bouffon; Chameau; L'Echo; Flash; Le Fou-rire; Hush; lei Montreal; Jackie; Joker; Jour et Nuit; Midnight; Nouvelles et police judi-ciaire; La Pie; Rigolade; Le Trou de la serrure.
I denounce the publishers, printers and distributors who are responsible in great part for juvenile delinquency.
In the first list, issued in February 1958, there were 30 papers, nine of which no longer exist. In the second list, issued on May 23, 1958, there were 25 papers, thirteen of which are no longer published. The third list contains the 16 papers that I have just named, and I hope that all of them will cease publication. I strongly urge municipal authorities and police, Catholic and Protestant organizations, to join in denouncing those publications and in alerting the authorities concerned so that people responsible for this situation may be brought before the courts.
In conclusion, I wish to refer to papers of May 12, 1960 and especially to Le Devoir-

I know that La Presse mentioned it also- where Cardinal Leger is reported to have said to Holy Name societies:
The fight against obscene publications must go on unremittingly.
It must be waged by all social classes, by all those who want morality to be respected and who want to eradicate obscene publications. And, after the hon. member for Laurier, I would remind you that a wave of criminality is now sweeping the North American continent, and I repeat, perhaps the main cause of it is that bad literature.
I wanted to take this opportunity to denounce bad literature and ask all honest and responsible people to see that people responsible for such a tragic situation are brought before the courts.

I would be remiss, Mr. Chairman, if I were to delay unduly the business of the house, but I believe this is the right opportunity to congratulate, first of all, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) for the excellent news he gave the Canadian people on or about June 15 of last year, when he informed us that his department would introduce a bill to modify the Bankruptcy Act which was enacted as far back as 1949.
The present Bankruptcy Act has become a disgrace for every businessman and the people in general. It is surprising to note the growing number of bankruptcies, but we may not stop to find out the main reasons for those business failures or why debtors are led to defraud-and I stress that word-to defraud their creditors.
Unfortunately, there are too many public trustees-and when I say that, I would like to exclude the public trustees of the judicial districts of Three Rivers or Joliette, with whom I have had many transactions with regard to the administration of the Bankruptcy Act-but unfortunately too many public trustees are seeking insolvent debtors, or people struggling with their creditors- and urging them to assign their property or chattels, often demanding up to a thousand dollars to free those debtors of all liability towards their creditors under the present provisions of the Bankruptcy Act.
I know, sir, that particular attention will be brought to the various recommendations that will be submitted to you by the various organizations, by the Canadian Bar Association, and by the various rural bar associations. However, may I suggest or, at least, call
Supply-Justice
the attention of relevant officials in your department to the fact that there should be, first of all, a change in the definition now found in section 2, paragraph (n) of the Bankruptcy Act, where the legislator defines the expression: "insolvent person" as meaning someone who owes a thousand dollars or more. That provision, which was applicable and appropriate in 1949, has now become entirely unjustified, and I think that it would be much more fitting to impose more costly terms on those who, through dishonesty, fraud or otherwise, too often hide behind the provisions of the legislation now in effect to cheat with impunity creditors who had trusted them in their capacity of business or professional men.
I also would be remiss not to commend the minister for his attitude with regard to the numerous public trustees who lack honesty in the exercise of their profession. I know the appropriate officers of your department are continuing their investigation to halt this bankruptcy threat, this tremendous surge of debtors who today assign their property not in the interest of their creditors but to protect the possessions they have accumulated, and make use of the act to gratify their greed and demands.
I think an excellent suggestion might be to amend section 20 and require any debtor wishing to assign his property to appear before a proper judge, perhaps of the superior court, and state the reasons forcing him to assign his property. After an investigation which might be conducted by the judge, the judge alone would decide when and under what conditions the debtor could file a petition in bankruptcy. At that time, the judge, on the basis of his investigation and of the facts as ascertained by him, would be in a position either to refuse or grant to the debtor authorization to file a petition in bankruptcy.
Unfortunately, under the present provisions of the act-I would not want to appear in any way to be casting aspersions on the decisions our judges have rendered so far -judges are too generous, that is to say, they tend to be too soft in discharging debtors of their debts.
I think the provisions of section 130 should be amended to provide that no debtor can be discharged unless he has paid at least 50 per cent of what he owes his creditors.
Moreover, the Bankruptcy Act should contain a provision barring any debtor from

Supply-Justice
being discharged of a debt arising out of a misdemeanour or a technical offence. Too often today-in the province of Quebec, for instance, and probably elsewhere-a debtor having to meet obligations arising out of a rather costly judgment for liability in an automobile accident, easily avoids his liability by filing a petition in bankruptcy and then obtaining his release, thus being dispensed from the necessity of abiding by the provisions of the judgment, and, too often, unfortunately, to the detriment of a widow or orphans.
I know, Mr. Minister, that in due course, you will introduce a bill to remedy such a situation, one which has lasted too long, so that honest people who, in the pursuit of their business, meet with difficulties that prevent them from honouring their obligations, may avail themselves of the provisions of that new bankruptcy act, but also in order that dishonest debtors who are taking advantage of the provisions of the present act to defraud their creditors, may not find an easy refuge to satisfy their greed and hang on to their property.
Furthermore, I think it would benefit the Canadian economy if the provisions of that act were amended so as to provide more rigorous restrictions designed to put an end to present abuses.

Mr. Chairman, I have three matters to raise briefly on this first item but I shall rise on three different occasions so that the subjects will not become merged in the minister's mind. First of all I want to express my appreciation at the courtesy and attention the minister has given to any question I have brought to his notice and for his promptness on all occasions.
Before proceeding with my few brief remarks I want to express my support for the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East and my admiration for the way he has carried on over a period of 25 years his work and interest, and his attention particularly to those unfortunate persons who use narcotics and those who require rehabilitation after imprisonment. In British Columbia the work he has done in that respect is recognized by members of all parties and I think it is only right to bring that to the attention of the committee now.
I am now bringing to the attention of the minister a question which has been brought to my attention by a number of persons, one person in particular through correspondence and others who have discussed the matter

with me in my office who are concerned with the administration of justice. They charge that there is illegal confinement and treatment of prisoners in Bordeaux jail. I raise this on the minister's estimates because I understand that according to the revised statutes of 1952 the Governor General is held responsible for any injustice suffered by any person in Canada, and if that is correct then I presume there is a degree of responsibility on the part of the minister.
The great philosopher Justinian said that justice is the constant and perpetual wish to render to every man his due. Because I am fully confident that the minister agrees with that statement wholeheartedly I also raise a matter which has been discussed over the radio of Quebec, in television programs and elsewhere. On October 30 last there was a very interesting article in La Presse entitled: "The Minister of Health Promises to Correct the Abnormal Situation in One Year." That has to do with what is termed the scandal at Bordeaux. I just wish to quote briefly a paragraph or two from correspondence which I have received in order to bring the matter to the attention of the committee. This is from a letter which I received from a gentleman on November 10, 1959 of this year. He says:
I am enclosing a clipping from La Presse of Friday, October 30. This is a story of another person whom they had incarcerated without a hearing in Bordeaux jail for a mental examination, and for three years certain persons who have become interested have been trying to get him out since he has never been properly examined by a psychiatrist, and no evidence has ever been given that he was unbalanced.
Then on May 30, the same person wrote to me as follows:
About a month ago you wrote you were going to question the minister regarding this case of the man who had been in Bordeaux for five years without ever appearing in court. I was wondering what the result of the questioning was. Nothing has been done here since I last wrote.
I bring this matter to the attention of the minister and would like his comment with respect to the case. I have quite a voluminous correspondence in connection with this subject. Two or three other persons from Montreal have sent me letters in connection with it, and they feel very disturbed about it.
Finally, I have another case I should like to bring to the attention of the minister and to explain it I will just quote from a newspaper cutting dated January 15 which appeared in the Montreal Star. It is headed: "Court Frees Girl Held Three Weeks", and reads:
A 16-year old girl was liberated yesterday by a sessions court judge of a charge of obstructing

the course of justice, stemming from a shooting last October in a St. Antoine street rooming house.
Said Judge M. A. Blain in freeing the slight, pale-faced girl: "I have looked into the evidence carefully and I feel certain that no jury would convict on the evidence produced. You are liberated ..."
When the preliminary hearing started Tuesday, defence lawyer Clair Barrette claimed the girl had been kept in jail since her arrest more than three weeks ago and had not been arraigned within the 24-hour delay prescribed by law.
Judge Blain ordered police prosecutors present to see to it that the law was observed to the letter in such matters. This was promised.
I simply put this on record so that the minister may be in possession of this information with respect to this girl who apparently did not receive justice according to the criminal law of this country. Then again there is the case of the incarceration in Bordeaux of the person I mentioned, and I may add that another person who spoke to me told me there were nine or ten similar cases.
That is all I have to say at this time, though I may rise again to deal with other matters in the course of the discussion.

924 days,-924 days, without knowing why.

It therefore appears that, in Canada, an individual may spend a certain time in prison without his case being brought to court and without preliminary inquiry, and, moreover, without knowing why he is imprisoned.
Mr. Chairman, that is a rather unique situation, you will admit. I am not blaming the minister, for it was the author's design to draw his attention to that situation without reproaching him for it. Besides, I shall be reading, in a minute, his opinion of the minister.
On page 12 we find the following:
Even if that scandal were the only one-"But it is not the only one" . ..
... there are hundreds of them in the prisons and mental institutions of the province of Quebec. Human beings, sons of the Catholic Church, British subjects, Canadian citizens, they are brothers to all men who are being mocked, humiliated, persecuted and unjustly detained in the dungeons of Budapest, Madrid, Ciudad Trujillo or Vladivostok. And they are our own brothers, those who suffer most, those whom abbe Pierre insists must be served first.
The book goes on to recite facts which, astonishingly, are taking place here in Canada.
On page 142, there is a reference to the minister. I quote:
However, it seems obvious to me that one of the most acute problems, one which lies at the basis of several others, is the overcrowded condition of our penitentiaries in general and of Bordeaux jail in particular.
At the federal level, Hon. Davie Fulton himself has denounced the scandal and announced a rigorous program which, within two years, should put an end to it. At the provincial level the scandal is infinitely more spectacular, but government authorities remain inactive and consider the matter as taboo. And yet, a newspaper generally in sympathy with the present regime dared write, only a few months ago:
Then follows a description of a situation I would not like to record in Hansard, because it refers to the appalling conditions that exist there:	Overcrowding, unsatisfactory
hygienic conditions.
Those two points deserve the attention of the authorities. The minister has probably received a copy of the book and, on reading parts of it, must have realized what inhuman conditions are imposed upon the prisoners.
We know that the minister is sympathetic and is aware of the basic nature of the problem.
He is frequently in touch with the various attorneys general. We know that as Minister of Justice, he wants to heed the conclusions of the Fauteux report. In fact, so far he has followed many of its recommendations.
However, because of present conditions, may I be allowed to urge the minister and his officials not only to read the book again

but especially to fully grasp the nature of the conditions to which prisoners are subjected at Bordeaux jail.
While it is true that since the book came out, and even before that, the governor of the jail introduced certain improvements, the fact remains that, in spite of those improvements, the situation is serious indeed, and to the extent where the minister can and must remedy that shocking situation, I urge him to do so.
