Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a brief plea on behalf of judges' salaries but prior to doing that may I congratulate and commend the minister and his department on the improvements in the penal system which he has initiated and which will be of great benefit to this country and long remembered after he and every member in this house will have left for that country from which no man has ever returned.
I think it is very interesting that in England about 100 years ago, the country from which our common law is derived, at a time when doctors were in the same economic position and were considered to be in the class of barbers, judges, as soon as they were appointed, were immediately made law lords with all the prerogatives and privileges that were involved in that status. I think it is indisputable that since then both the doctors and the barbers have tended to inhabit the earth while the comparative status of judges,

economically and socially, has progressively tended to decline. I think their condition has been deteriorating over a period of say 50 years and I think it is notoriously difficult today to get lawyers of the first order, leading lawyers, to become judges despite the honour involved, because there is a tremendous financial sacrifice connected with the position. In many instances they would be obliged to accept about one quarter, perhaps, of what they had been accustomed to in the way of income. It is obvious that the administration of law and order is the basis of any society; it is the whole basis of any civilized society and it is of the utmost importance that we have the finest and most able men available in the country on the bench. There is no job of greater importance than that of our judges.
When the ordinary citizen goes before the courts his respect and attitude toward law and order and toward government is largely determined by the fairness and the objectivity of the hearing that he gets from the judges at various levels. It is also commonplace that judges daily are called upon to adjudicate matters involving millions of dollars. If those same judges are preoccupied with maintaining their livelihood they cannot give the detachment that is required to their onerous duties.
There is also one other aspect which I mentioned at another time in the house. We tend to be living in a materialistic age where there appears to be a price tag on everything. Often a man's worth tends, unfortunately, inevitably, to be judged more on his income than on anything else. If that is so, and I think it is substantially true, it puts our judges in an unfair and untenable position.
I reiterate, it is essential that we have the best men available on the bench and we must offer sufficient inducement so they can be attracted to this most honourable position and, having attained this position, they should be relieved of the mundane cares and there should be nothing to deprive them of their integrity and objectivity.
As I have mentioned before, I think the same thing applies to members of parliament and members of government as to judges. Neither those on the bench nor those in this house, because of inadequacy of income, should ever degenerate into the position where the bench or this house would be a rich man's club or the refuge of the destitute.

I should like to make a few brief remarks on a number of subject matters in which I have interest, one of which, of course, is being discussed in the banking and commerce committee at the moment. Perhaps this will be to a degree restricted to the things that may be engaged in by the combines investigation branch.
Supply-Justice
I should like to make reference to the question of penal institutions, the attitude of the minister with respect to penitentiaries and penology, and to express appreciation of the forward looking view that the minister has on these questions. At one time not too many years ago the view held was that incarceration in a penitentiary was purely a method or form of punishment and nothing else. The view was that if a person committed a crime and was convicted what would accrue to him would be punishment and that was all, that punishment was an end in itself.
But there has been a change in this attitude over the years, a change that is still under way. I think more people are coming to the point of view that we should concern ourselves more with the after-effects of a penitentiary sentence rather than just thinking in terms of getting someone out of the way because he or she has committed a particular crime. The changing of our thinking toward rehabilitating people who have been convicted of crimes and the bending of our efforts toward reformation need to be strengthened from time to time, and I think we continually have to work toward that goal.
The reformation and rehabilitation process takes place in two fields. One is while the inmate is in the penitentiary and the other is after the inmate is released on parole or under some other arrangement. In the latter case after-care agencies are involved whose aim is to ensure that the person gets back into the social structure and remains outside of the penitentiary for the rest of his life. However, there is an obstacle in the way of dealing effectively with the rehabilitative or reformative process and that obstacle lies in the penitentiaries themselves.
The minister has made the comment a number of times that he is thoroughly conversant and familiar with the overcrowding in our penitentiaries. He has visited them and seen the situation, as have other members.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. member whether he does not consider that discussion would be better served if matters having to do with penitentiaries and correctional reform were deferred until we reach item 161? I intend to make a general statement on our penal reform program and on the present situation in the penitentiaries on that item. I had hoped that we could confine the present item to a general discussion of the Department of Justice itself and have a general discussion of penitentiaries on item 161 and a general discussion of the R.C.M.P., if desired, on the first item under that heading.

Supply-Justice

Certainly I do not mind. The minister will appreciate that I was absent when discussion of these estimates started because the banking and commerce committee was meeting. I do not mind doing so at all. In fact, I think it would perhaps be a better way to approach the matter. We always look upon the administration item as one affording an opportunity for a far-ranging debate on all phases of the work of the department. I would be glad to defer my remarks about penitentiaries until we reach that item. In the light of past practice I had come to the conclusion that the minister, as other ministers are wont to do, had made general opening remarks covering the subject matter but if that is not the case perhaps it would be better for me to delay my remarks until I can relate them to what the minister has to say on the subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It might be interesting to give the reason why I have suggested two or three times this afternoon that this pattern of discussion should be followed, namely that penitentiaries should be dealt with under item 161 and the R.C.M.P. under item 372. The position actually is that the department constituted under the Department of Justice Act has a deputy minister as the senior administrative officer and when the first item we are now on, 151, is called, the deputy minister and the departmental officials attend. The penitentiaries branch has as its senior administrative officer the commissioner of penitentiaries who actually has the status of a deputy minister, and when that item is reached it is the practice for the commissioner of penitentiaries to come here with other officials to assist me in the discussion. The senior official of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is the commissioner whose position is created by statute and therefore the commissioner attends here with his officers when that item is reached.
In my recollection that has been the general pattern of discussion and it seems to me that the best way of enabling me to deal with the questions and comments made by hon. members is if they will raise them in that order. The hon. member for Vancouver East did point out that he wanted to make some remarks about penitentiaries because he had to leave the house and might not be back, but I think I will defer replying to his comments until we reach the penitentiaries item.
May I attempt to deal briefly with what has been said by hon. members who have spoken on this item. I can assure the hon. member for Megantic that I appreciate, as do the deputy minister and one of the assistant deputies who are leaving the department,

his comments, with which I fully agree, our views and our regrets having already been expressed by the Prime Minister when he announced the resignations. Although I know he is going to be embarrassed and that one does not usually mention civil servants individually, I think under these circumstances I may be permitted to indulge in an exception which proves the rule and point out that it is perhaps appropriate that the last official act of my deputy minister is to be here on the floor of the house when the estimates of the Department of Justice are under consideration. I think it is appropriate and fitting somehow that on his last day of service with the department he should be in the House of Commons with the minister dealing with matters with which he is so familiar and in the shaping of which he has played such a large and valuable part.
The hon. member next dealt with the question of the reason for the increase in the number of judges in the Montreal district. I think he will agree with me that since there was a reasonably full discussion of that matter when the Judges Act amendments were before us it is not appropriate for me to go into any detail on that subject. I think the discussion has been full indeed. I appreciate the interest of the hon. member in raising the matter at this time, his concern being mainly to make the point that the increase in criminality in the province of Quebec is certainly no greater than anywhere else. That, of course, was recognized although I did point out that the increase in a certain type of crime, crimes of violence, is causing the greatest concern to the authorities in Montreal and properly so.
The hon. member for Vancouver East dealt with a number of items that mainly concern the penitentiaries branch but he did discuss the question of narcotics. He raised the question of what should be the general approach to the narcotic problem and asked me to outline the point we have reached in the shaping of a new policy, to which I have myself referred on a number of occasions. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre also discussed narcotics in a constructive and obviously well informed and thoughtful manner. Perhaps I could say a word or two about that subject at this time.
As I announced recently, we have now been able to advance our studies to the point where a new government policy for dealing with the problem of the criminal narcotic addict has been worked out. This policy has been approved by the cabinet and inasmuch as it involves, necessarily if it is to be fully implemented and serve the useful purpose which we hope it will serve, the co-operation of the

provinces, the authority was also given to have the officials of my department communicate with the provincial officials for preliminary discussions. This has been done in the case of British Columbia recently when informal discussions were held with the deputy attorney general of that province. An outline of the approach and of the policy was left with him, and we expect and hope shortly to be hearing from British Columbia about arrangements for further positive and constructive discussions.
I expect shortly to be making arrangements for the initial approach to the other provinces mainly concerned, that is the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. I outlined in a release accompanying the announcement of policy the broad terms of our approach. I think perhaps it would be appropriate for me to mention them here also.
It is our conclusion that although the number of criminal addicts in Canada is not in itself large, about 3,500, and although the number has been constant as was indicated by the figures put on the record by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, nevertheless this is one of the greatest single instances of social waste that one could imagine. My information is that of this number of addicts, at any one time about one third of them are in the process of going through our penal institutions, and although the number does not increase it is a sort of constantly revolving flow. This seems to prove two things, at least: first, that there is this situation, an unsupportable social waste, the details of which will be too obvious to need elaboration; second, and perhaps more important, that the methods we are now following in dealing with the problem, by punishing addicts and then releasing them at the end of their sentence to re-enter the stream, is completely useless when looked at from the point of view of whether we are curing the evil. Obviously, we are not even beginning to deal with it.
We came to the conclusion, therefore, that a new approach was necessary. Instructions were given to the officials of my department, together with those of welfare, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the penitentiaries branch, to work out a new approach which might have more hope of providing a constructive answer to this problem. The approach which they have now worked out, and which we have approved in principle in so far as the federal responsibility is concerned, is based on two main principles; first, on treatment while in custody and, second, on supervision after release.
In the past there has been, at least in federal institutions, no real attempt to treat the narcotic addict in so far as what
Supply-Justice
might be described as his medical situation is concerned; no attempt to cure him of his addiction. There is, of course, withdrawal and complete separation from narcotics while in the penitentiary, but no real program of attempting to find the medical causes and cures, if any, for that tendency to addiction from which he suffers. This, therefore, will be one of the changed elements in the federal program for the treatment of narcotic offenders when that program is worked out.
First, there will be provision made for treatment while in custody and, second,- although this is perhaps not a startlingly new approach-there should be segregation in special type institutions while undergoing the treatment. This segregation of narcotic addicts from other types of criminals will have more than one advantage. It minimizes at least, indeed should end, the danger of contamination of non-addicts by criminal addicts, while at the same time providing a scientifically designed centre for the treatment of addicts in so far as they are capable of treatment in the medical and psychological sense.
I come then to the question of what should be done with the addicts after they have served their sentences. This brings me to the second main division of the new approach. It is my understanding that the weight of medical evidence shows that it is never safe to regard a narcotic addict as completely cured. This fact will of course not minimize the efforts we are going to make to treat him effectively while in custody.
It seems to us that one of the great weaknesses of the present method of handling this problem is that the criminal narcotic addict, sometimes a man with a long history of addiction, is discharged from the penitentiary and apart from the ordinary efforts that may be made by after-care agencies to assist him in finding employment, and so on, there is no special post-release supervision. It is our view that this is a definite lack, and as long as it continues there will be a gap in the program. If it is a fact that a narcotic addict can never be safely regarded as completely cured; he is always going to have a tendency to yield to temptation and return to his addiction. If we could, by a program of post-discharge supervision, both encourage the addict to go straight as well as supervise his habits, we could help him to keep away from narcotics.
It is our view, accordingly, that the law should make provision for a lengthy period of supervision after the termination of his sentence. This will have two effects. First,

Supply-Justice
it will, I hope, give the man a sense that he is not alone; that he has not been discharged and left to his own resources to resist the temptation to return to addiction. There is somebody there to whom he can turn for help in resisting this tendency. Second, it will serve the obviously useful purpose of providing somebody to counsel and assist the man in finding suitable employment and also assist him in meeting some of the problems to which perhaps the narcotic addict is especially exposed, problems of a psychological as well as a physical nature.
These are the two main principles of the new approach, the new emphasis on treatment and segregation while in the institution and on supervision after release into society. There are a number of other minor and consequential changes which will follow. For instance, in line with the same sort of thinking as was expressed by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, namely, that the drug trafficker should also have his sentence suit the circumstances of his crime, it would be our proposal to amend the act so that a life sentence might be imposed even for the first offence; I refer not to a mandatory life sentence but to a provision that there could be a sentence of imprisonment for life even on the first offence. That will depend, of course, on the circumstances and the nature of the crime.
I have mentioned our feeling that for the complete success of our narcotic program it is essential to have the full co-operation of the provinces. The reason for that is this. We can deal with the narcotic addict only when he is a criminal and after he has been convicted of a criminal offence. That is the only circumstance in which the federal authority has jurisdiction. We may be successful -and I certainly hope and believe that we shall be-in the new program when we have it implemented. Again I must caution that these things cannot be done over night. It is going to take time. We must provide new institutions or new types of institutions, for one thing. However, when we get it going it is our belief that we will be successful in dealing with the problem of the addict after he has become a criminal and with the problem of treating him and then giving him a chance to return and live a useful life in society.
But that will be dealing with only half the problem because it does not touch the problem of the person who is an addict without being a criminal; nor does it touch the problem of the person who is of that physical or psychological nature which makes him likely to be an addict; and it does not touch the problem of helping him not to become an addict. This problem can, in fact, be

tackled only by the provincial authorities because they are the ones who have jurisdiction in cases of that type. We would therefore be dealing as a nation with only half of the problem if it is dealt with only on the basis of the approach to the criminal narcotic addict.
While the problem of the criminal narcotic addict is a grave one and, in so far as the individual is concerned, a terrible one, it is in a sense if not a part, perhaps an outgrowth of another and perhaps even larger problem, namely the problem of delinquency. Studies that have been made over the years have convinced my officials that it can safely be said of the generality of the criminal narcotic addicts that they are delinquents first and addicts second because in the vast majority of cases there is a history of delinquency, and usually juvenile delinquency, before there is a history of criminal narcotic addiction; that is to say, the history of one man shows that he was first a juvenile delinquent before he became a criminal narcotic addict.
This matter relates to the problem of increasing criminality mentioned by the hon. member for Laurier and upon which I might say a word or two in a moment. But we are now dealing with the special aspect of that problem related to delinquency. Again, the federal government does not acquire jurisdiction until some crime is committed. The authorities having the most immediate approach and opportunity are, of course, the home, the school and the church-they are the ones who first come into contact with young people-supplemented as they should be by the efforts of municipal and provincial governments to create moral and ethical training and physical environment which will go a long way toward preventing delinquency and, where it does not prevent it, then toward dealing with the problem of delinquency.
There is also the question of how to deal with the person who becomes an addict but has not yet been convicted of it and therefore is not what I call a criminal addict. As I have said, we do not get jurisdiction until he is convicted and is a criminal addict or a criminal and an addict. The only people who can deal with this problem again are the provinces. It is our view that there should be centres to which persons who are addicts but are not criminals may be committed for treatment. Again, only the provinces have the jurisdiction and the authority to provide these centres and to provide, by legislation or otherwise, the circumstances under which a person may be committed to those centres for treatment or assistance.

In summary, then, our approach is that we believe there should be a program in the federal jurisdiction of treatment in segregation and treatment in custody and supervision and care after release from custody. We believe that within the provincial field there should be a program of institutions to which a man may be committed for treatment even before he becomes a criminal and where he may be encouraged to end his addiction in order that he may have a better chance of leading a non-criminal life. Indeed, over and above that concrete type of program-I refer to the institutional types of programs-we believe there should be greater emphasis on those measures necessary to prevent and to deal with the problem of delinquency so as to prevent criminality before it is too late.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall vote 151 carry?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I really had just concluded my statement dealing with narcotics. There were a number of other matters that were dealt with and I think I would be discourteous if I did not refer to them.
The hon. member for Laurier mentioned the problem of growing criminality generally. What I have said in connection with the problem of narcotics I think covers that field at least as fully as I am capable of covering it. It is partly a moral problem. It involves the ethics of all levels of society including the parent, the home, the school, the church, the educational institutions, the provincial institutions and what we can do by way of treatment, et cetera in criminal institutions. But federal jurisdiction arises only after the crime has been committed. In connection with the comment of the hon. member for Laurier that there was some concern lest the growing criminality in points like Montreal was owing to the fact that the penitentiary was in close proximity to the city, I must say that it does not seem to me to be well taken. Discharged criminals just like free persons will inevitably tend to go back to those places where they feel most at home; and even if we removed the penitentiary from Montreal, we are obliged to return a prisoner to the place from which he came, the place at which he was convicted or in special cases to some other place if he says that he wants to go some other place. I therefore do not think the removal of a penitentiary physically from Montreal would make any difference in that regard.
Then the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere dealt with the problem of bankruptcy administration generally and with one or two particular features of it. I should like to assure him at the outset that I appreciate greatly what he said and I
Supply-Justice
think he put his finger squarely on the problem when he described the evil represented by the type of unethical trustee who will solicit estates, say, on this basis; you pay me $500 or $1,000 and I can get you discharged from all your debts; you will be scot-free from then on, and you can go back into business again. This, of course, is the root of the problem. I regret that we have a number of trustees who carry on in that way. It has taken us some time to isolate them. We were obliged to institute an inquiry within a reasonable time after 1957. This inquiry brought to light a number of very disturbing circumstances in connection with the administration of certain trustees.
We have now taken steps which I think represent an approach to dealing with the problem. First, we have a number of prosecutions under way. I am not able to say very much specifically because the cases have not yet been disposed of and it would be improper for me to make any comment or to draw any conclusions before the courts have said whether our charges are properly founded or not. But we have a number of prosecutions under way which I think is an indication of our intention to clear up this question.
Second, in addition to the prosecutions which are actually before the courts in which charges have been laid we have a really quite wide scale investigation under way into the activities of trustees generally.
Third, we have recently introduced a tightening up, if you like, of the investigation into the circumstances under which we appoint trustees and as to the qualifications of trustees.
Fourth, as I indicated in a speech I made in Winnipeg recently, we do intend at the first convenient time possible to undertake a general review of the Bankruptcy Act. Whilst at Winnipeg I took the advantage, when addressing the Canadian credit men's trust association, to ask for their recommendations as to how a number of these problems might be dealt with and as to how we might improve the administration of the Bankruptcy Act, as well as how we might possibly amend or revise the act itself.
I should say in conclusion here that we can only undertake so many reforms at one time, and while these are our intentions and while we have made some preliminary approaches which I have outlined, I want to sound a note of caution that I am not suggesting that the Bankruptcy Act is going to be revised tomorrow, because as I say these matters require a great deal of careful study before one is in a position to suggest complete revisions to parliament. But I think I may

Supply-Justice
say that rather more than the preliminary steps have been taken and are under way leading toward an improvement in the situation.
One final matter in this field. I could not agree more than I do with the hon. member when he said, in effect, that he felt the judges should be more careful, more strict if you like, in dealing with applications for the discharge of bankrupts. I know the judges are very busy and that only certain judges perhaps are specialists in this field and therefore the burden on them is very great; but I can do no more than express the hope that our judges will also realize there have been abuses by unethical trustees and that they will do all they can to ensure when an application for discharge is made before them that not only all that can be done to satisfy the just claims of creditors has been done, but that the administration by the trustees has been proper and ethical in accordance with the terms of the Bankruptcy Act.
The hon. member for Kootenay West, whose comments I always appreciate and for which I wish to thank him, brought to my attention the case of a man who it was alleged had been committed to Bordeaux jail having, as I understood it, been charged with a criminal offence, who had then been committed to that jail as an insane person, and as a result had never been able to obtain a hearing either with respect to his insanity or to obtain a trial to deal with the criminal offence with which he was originally charged.
The hon. member also referred to the case of a girl, in I believe that same jail, with respect to whom there had been a very great delay in bringing her up for preliminary hearing in connection with the criminal charge against her.
I regret that all I can say with regard to both these cases is that the responsibility there is entirely provincial. I can do nothing more than bring the cases and these complaints to the attention of the provincial attorney general if I am provided with the details, and I will ask him or suggest to him that he might feel it proper to make an investigation.
This is because the administration of criminal law is the responsibility of provincial officials. It is true that our Criminal Code provides that no person can be held in custody for more than 24 hours, if my recollection is right, without a charge being laid or a remand being asked for which gives an opportunity for the person to be brought before the magistrate. There are various other provisions designed to safeguard the person, but the administration of all those provisions

is the responsibility of provincial officials, as is also the administration of provincial jails such as Bordeaux. Indeed, by the constitution the management of provincial jails is specifically vested in the provincial governments, and again the provisions with regard to the circumstances under which people may be committed to institutions on grounds of mental illness are all controlled by provincial statute. We have no jurisdiction in that field.
Therefore I am necessarily confined to answering by saying that the investigation of the complaints made here would lie within the field of provincial responsibility, and all 1 can do is to bring such complaints as may be brought to my attention in turn to the attention of the attorney general of that province with the suggestion that he might feel it appropriate to investigate.
I am afraid the same general remarks must be made in reply to the hon. member for Laurier when he intervened the second time in the discussion this afternoon with specific reference to a book, which I believe was written by a Mr. Hebert, regarding the conditions in Bordeaux jail. I have had this book drawn to my attention, but again I can only say that the conditions in Bordeaux jail are exclusively the responsibility of the provincial government. Paragraph 6 of section 92 of the British North America Act is the provision in question here, and it provides that amongst those things coming within the exclusive jurisdiction of the province are the establishment, maintenance and management of public and reformatory prisons in and for the province.
So that while I appreciate the remarks of the hon. member for Laurier and accept them in the spirit in which he made them, with regard to his suggestion that, so far as it lay within my power, I might look into this matter and the allegations made in the book, I am nevertheless compelled to answer and must answer that it does not lie in any sense within my power. Indeed it lies completely outside my power except again that I can draw the attention of the provincial officials to the fact that the book has been written, the allegations have been made and that they might care to investigate.
1 think it is also proper for me to suggest to the hon. member for Laurier that if, indeed, he feels it is incumbent upon somebody to make an investigation, then since it is not within my power may I remind him that those who I believe are much more friendly to him than was the former government of Quebec will, if I read the indications properly, or shortly will have responsibility

in that province and he can bring his representations and his request for an investigation forward to them with much greater effect and with much more practicality than he would be showing when he suggests that I make an investigation into a provincial jail.
I think that covers pretty well all of that which was said by hon. members in this discussion so far, with the exception of the hon. member for Stormont whose comments on judges' salaries I must say in general I agree with.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened to the outline given by the minister of the problem of narcotic addiction and his views relative to it. I cannot agree more with the minister that as far as the federal jurisdiction is concerned, even if the federal authority does go ahead as the minister outlined with special institutions for treatment of narcotic addicts, it only touches half the problem and that the other half lies completely within the jurisdiction of the provincial authorities.
What I would like to ask and to get clear in my mind is this. Has the minister made representations to the provincial authorities asking for the introduction of a policy that there should be the use of the same institutions, or similar institutions, in which narcotic addicts of a non-criminal nature could be handled in two ways? In other words, I should like to know if in the mind of the minister there is a policy that provincially the addict who is not a criminal can voluntarily submit himself for treatment. Does the minister feel, as I certainly do, that if a noncriminal addict declines to submit himself voluntarily he can be picked up and given the necessary treatment under provincial legislation to that end.
I am very serious in holding this view, because hon. members will remember that a few years ago in British Columbia tuberculosis was getting completely out of hand. Then a law was brought down that if a person who had active tuberculosis did not voluntarily submit himself for treatment he could be picked up and given the treatment. Today, as is well known, they are closing the tuberculosis hospitals in Vancouver and only about one-third of the available beds are being used in the one hospital that remains open. Some might take the view and, indeed, they would be right, that in legislation of this kind we are moving into the realm of civil rights. But in my opinion there is no infringing of the civil rights of an individual when it is being done not only for his own benefit but for the protection of the majority.
Supply-Justice
I confidently hope that the provincial authorities will move in this direction and that treatment of addicts may proceed upon these dual lines.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am glad to be able to say that in general the approach outlined by the hon. member coincides with that recommended by my officials to me and in turn to the cabinet and approved in principle by the cabinet. He will appreciate that what is done at the provincial level is entirely for their decision but it has been recommended to us that we discuss with them the possibility of working out together and implementing in our respective spheres an approach along those lines. It would be our thought that if we get agreement with the provinces along these lines then since we are bound to provide for a number of addicts in any event in our institution, we would hope, as soon as we can physically do it, to provide these special institutions, as I said earlier, and since we have to provide them in any event we would make them available under proper safeguards and on proper terms for the committal of addicts, if the provinces agree. Thus we would only need the one institution to treat addicts.
It is also our thought that if the legislation, federal, provincial or both, could be so framed as to provide for voluntary admission, or the admission of persons to come voluntarily for treatment in these institutions, it is certainly our hope that there will be provincial legislation complementary to the legislation which we shall ultimately introduce here to provide for the treatment of addicts who do not volunteer and who are, after proper inquiry, committed to these institutions.
It seems to me that in general the approach is somewhat similar to that with respect to mental illness. If it is believed that somebody is suffering from mental illness which may make him dangerous, most provincial legislatures have provided that after a proper inquiry, certification by properly qualified medical men, he may be committed for treatment in an institution. It seems to us that the same approach forms the basis of what we have in the narcotics field as well.

The question which I have in mind to address to the minister is one which could, perhaps, wait until the next item is reached, but if I raise it now the hon. gentleman will have an opportunity to answer it in his introductory remarks.
It comes to me from the John Howard society in Saskatoon which, as the minister knows, is a society which has been in existence there for a number of years as well as in other parts of the country. They have

Supply-Justice
been very pleased with the selections that have been made in connection with the national parole board and their representatives express the view that progress is being made as a result of the establishment of the national parole board. They say it is true that parole is a privilege and not a right. It is based not on any form of clemency or forgiveness, nor is it designed as a reward for good conduct in the institution. The emphasis is on rehabilitation. These people are told to serve the rest of their sentences in the community under the guidance of counsellors.
The society goes on to point out the savings to the taxpayer which can be made by using the provisions which have been set up. An example is given from the state of Pennsylvania where it was found that by the extension of a similar type of parole the net saving in 1958 amounted to $137,865 in respect to 137 prisoners, or a gain of over $1,000 per person.
I say this to state the basis for the societies concerned that the program should be properly understood by the public at large. The society feels it is necessary to do an educational job so that the public may understand that this is not a soft policy which is being introduced but a scheme which in the long run will give them greater protection and enable a larger number of those discharged from prison to come back to society and become self-supporting.
The society concerned with an educational program is, I think, one that will present itself to the minister. 1 hope that in dealing with the item he will be able to tell us what steps are being taken to provide information along these lines to the general public and also to the various societies such as the John Howard society in order that they may carry on educational programs on their own in this connection.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to bring to the attention of the committee and again to the attention of the minister a matter concerning which I have spoken to him. I do so with the hope and expectation that it will receive serious consideration and that at the first opportunity a remedy will be provided. I have reference to what I consider to be a needed amendment to the present section 170 of the Criminal Code. I think I should put the section on the record as it now reads:
(1)	For the purpose of proceedings under this part, a place that is found to be equipped with a slot machine shall be conclusively presumed to be a common gaming house.
(2)	In this section "slot machine" means any automatic machine or slot machine
(a)	that is used or intended to be used for any purpose other than vending merchandise or services; or
(b)	that is used or intended to be used for the purpose of vending merchandise or services if
(i)	the result of one of any number of operations of the machine is a matter of chance or uncertainty to the operator,
(ii)	as a result of a given number of successive operations by the operator the machine produces different results, or
(iii)	on any operation of the machine it discharges or emits a slug or token.
I think I should also refer to section 176 of the code. I do so because I want to point out that what may be considered to be a somewhat minor or trivial matter does carry severe consequences. Section 176 reads:
(1) Every one who keeps a common gaming house or common betting house is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the first point I want to make very clearly is that I hold no brief whatsoever for gambling. That is not at all the object of my comments. In that connection I think I cannot better express my own views in so far as gambling is concerned than to quote the opinion of a justice in the United States who had this to say in his closing remarks on a case of this kind, after stating that he too was opposed to gambling:
However, the condemnation of gambling, or any other evil for that matter, should not be so loosely applied that it strikes down perfectly legitimate and innocuous pastimes. Many bridge players play for money but this would not justify the outlawing of bridge. Golf players sometimes make their game a little more dramatic by betting on the score but who would outlaw this healthful diversion because of a dollar or two which might change hands at the 18th hole? There is never a world series but that baseball enthusiasts wager on the results, but to condemn and outlaw the world series because fans bet on the scores, runs, hits, strike-outs and home runs emerging from any particular game or all of them would provoke millions of Americans to their feet crying injustice.
We know, of course, that the Criminal Code received consideration by a committee some few years ago, but in so far as this section is concerned I am satisfied that there
Suqply-Justice
was no intention and no belief on the part of those who introduced the codification of the Criminal Code at that time that there should be any change in the law in respect of slot machines. My view in that respect is borne out by a reference to Bill No. 7 as it was presented in the House of Commons at that time. Opposite section 170 there is merely the notation "Section 986 (4)", indicating that the new section was precisely the same as the old section but differently numbered.
If my view needs to be further strengthened may I refer to the debates of the House of Commons. I refer to page 2410 of Hansard of February 24, 1954, where the minister of justice at that time, Mr. Garson, had this to say:
But I would not admit for a moment that the law we are now considering is inadequate, because in substance it is a re-enactment of an existing section which had been in the code for a great many years.
Later, at page 2411, Mr. Brown, the hon. member for Brantford, asked this question of the minister:
Would the minister indicate whether there has been a change in the existing law?
The reply of the minister of justice of that time was:
Has my hon. friend read section 986 (4) of the Criminal Code?
Mr. Brown answered yes and Mr. Garson then replied:
I think if my friend will examine that-
Referring to section 986 (4).
-he will find that the substance is substantially the same as that of the present clause. I think it is put in a more intelligible form and in somewhat shorter compass.
I think that anyone who examines the two sections will agree, without reference to any judicial decisions which have been applied to the sections, that there has been a substantial change made in the law and that change relates to the application of those provisions of the old code which at that time were applicable only to machines which vended merchandise. The change made those provisions not only to those machines but also to machines vending only services which at that time and since have been held to include machines for amusement. That view was expressed in the recent judgment of Mr. Justice Ford. I will revert to that judgment a little later, but I wish to quote this portion of it to point out that there has been a change judicially established by this codification of the Criminal Code. After quoting section 170 he said:
I do not think it is necessary to quote the former subsection 986 (4). It is enough to point out that

Supply-Justice
170 (2) (a) of the present code . .. renders machines used or intended to be used for any purpose other than vending merchandise or services unlawful, as did subsection 986 (4), but in other respects the present subsection 170 (2) does not differ from the former subsection 986 (4) except that the re-enacted provisions are extended to apply also to a machine that is used or intended to be used for the purpose of vending services as well as one used or intended to be used for vending merchandise to which type of machine only the former subsection 986 (4) applied.
It strikes me it is a shocking situation that legislation should be enacted in the belief that no change is being made in the law when in reality a substantial change has been made. Just as an indication of the change that has been made in the law I should like to refer to a leading case on the subject, the case of Isseman v. the Queen, with which I am sure the Minister of Justice is quite familiar. This was a case that was carried up to the Supreme Court of Canada by the crown. The judgment to which I wish to refer is that of Mr. Justice Rand and the portion to which I wish to direct the attention of the committee is found on page 353 of Criminal Reports, volume 24. That portion reads as follows:
But the machine comes also within the language of paragraph (ii).
That is the paragraph that reads as follows:
(ii) as a result of any given number of successive operations by the operator the machine produces different results.
The judgment continues:
The results are the scores and different results are different scores. The contention faintly advanced was that "different results" are in relation to their nature and not mere dimensions in the same nature; that, for example, different results must exhibit, say, scores, prizes and goods as against differences in scores and that the paragraph does not apply. But I see nothing to support that contention. The scores are the objects aimed at and accomplished and in ordinary parlance they are as fully capable of exhibiting differences as other results provided by these or similar machines.
May I say that I only have reference to those machines which are generally known as amusement machines. I have no brief for and I am not making any argument on behalf of those machines which are used for gambling. I am only speaking of the innocent, innocuous machines such as those which you and I have played many times and which are not, in any sense, gambling machines. Perhaps I should refer to some significant words in this provision and they are that a place equipped with this type of machine shall be conclusively presumed to be a common gaming house.
I have always thought that under our British system of criminal jurisprudence a man was always presumed to be innocent

until he was proven guilty. There may be some exceptions which have crept into our law because of the apparent wickedness of certain commodities, per se, such as narcotics. Perhaps I should say that I cannot see the resemblance but we also put liquor in that category. In those cases, where possession of these things are considered to have some element of wickedness, the onus shifts, but it is always open to the accused to prove his innocence. There is no irrebuttable presumption against him.
Here we have a statute dealing with such innocuous things as amusement machines, such as those with which you and I have played many times, and we find that even though the machines are not used for gambling in any sense whatever-it may even be admitted by the crown that the machines are not used for gambling-nevertheless, because this statute says so, a magistrate has no option in the matter but to find the person guilty of something of which he is obviously not guilty. I say that any law on the statute books that convicts a person of an offence of which he is admittedly not guilty is a law that has no place in a British country, and certainly has no place in our Criminal Code.
We should not place those people who are found to be in possession of these innocuous machines under the stigma of being in the same category as the keeper of a disorderly house or a common bawdy house, which terms, of course, are analogous to a common gaming house. Such a person should not be subjected to a penalty as severe as two years in prison. I certainly do not want to keep the committee any longer than necessary, but I should like to make one further point.
The law, as it stands at the present time, I am informed, is not being enforced uniformly across this country. It does receive the approval, as I understand it, of certain attorneys general, but it does not receive the approval of others. I recognize that the Minister of Justice should have regard for the views of attorneys general, but I do not believe we should keep on our statute books, regardless of the views of attorneys general, a law which we in our wisdom believe should not be there. I strongly urge that this is a law in that category; that there should be amendments introduced which would exclude from its operation the machines to which I have made reference. I presume that those attorneys general who favour the retention of this law are naturally thinking of the enforcement problem in so far as gambling is concerned.
However, the fact that this law is not being uniformly enforced across the country does place in the hands of chiefs of police the right to put their finger upon one of these

operators and possibly have him sent to prison. I am not going to refer to any particular community, but I can say that there are communities in which the chiefs of police have taken action against the owners and keepers of these amusement machines, and they have been convicted of keeping a common gaming house. However, one of these chiefs of police has this kind of thing being displayed right in his own community: "Win $1,000 on home bingo". Can you think of anything that is more indicative of gambling than that kind of advertisement? Yet in that same community some individual keeping a game for amusement-a machine which could not be used for gambling and the most that could be won would be a free game-that person could be classed as a common criminal carrying on a common gaming house.
I say it is time that the hypocrisy ended. Either the law is good and serves a useful purpose or it should not be on the statute books. It should not be left to the whims and fancies of individuals to enforce it or not to enforce it, as they see fit. If we are opposed to gambling, let us be opposed to it in all its aspects. Let us not condone it in one situation and condemn it in another. There may be some who say, well it was not just because of gambling, I took this action because children may have been involved. This statute does not distinguish between adults and children. I did' not read the other section which deals with those who play the games, but under that section you or I may be convicted of being frequenters of a common gaming house merely because we were playing a game of amusement.
There is a great deal more I could say and a great deal more I should like to say. I am not one who is in favour of any machines that are used for gambling. Perhaps I should mention this further point. Despite this decision of the Supreme Court of Canada, I think there is considerable doubt as to whether or not that judgment applies to all these types of machines. I have read the judgment of Mr. Justice Rand and I believe it is so extensive that it covers all types of automatic machines. Certainly there have been convictions on the basis of its covering all types of machines and not all the convictions have been appealed.
I am happy to note that there is one case that went to the supreme court of Alberta. The judgment of Mr. Justice Ford to which I made reference a moment ago was a dissenting judgment. I believe in that case the course divided two and two and, as a result, the dismissal of the case by the magistrate stood. The magistrate perhaps looked at the case a little bit less from the standpoint of the law and more from the standpoint of 79951-0-354
Supply-Justice
common justice and dismissed it; but strictly on the basis of law he may be wrong. Nevertheless he did acquit. There has been a decision by the crown to appeal. I understand that the crown-that is to say, the attorney general-is not satisfied and that the case is coming to the Supreme Court of Canada.
Naturally the courts must determine the intention of parliament on the basis of the language that is used in the statute. It is not open to the court to look at what was said in the House of Commons. As far as the House of Commons is concerned, it is perfectly clear that the House of Commons never intended to change the law. That is something that has been made completely manifest. However, the court cannot look at that. They can look at the language we have used and the language we have used does not carry out the obvious intention of parliament. I think that is one matter that should receive the attention of the Minister of Justice and that some amendment should be made of this section. I believe the amendment which I have supplied to the minister eliminates only those machines that are not gambling machines and, in my opinion, are not capable of being used as gambling machines. It is those machines that I feel should be taken out of this category completely by an amendment, and I think that should be done at the earliest possible time.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a few remarks with regard to firearms.
The Minister of Justice is certainly aware that, very often, even every week, it is reported in our newspapers that our judges in criminal courts, and police court magistrates are protesting against the fact that today practically anybody, even teenagers, can secure firearms. This country's press, English or French speaking, has often stressed such complaints by our judges, and I think that public opinion also wants something to be done to restrict the possession of firearms and make the delivery of permits much more difficult.
Even if delivery of those permits is under the jurisdiction of the attorney general in each province, since the offence is provided for in the Criminal Code, and is therefore under federal jurisdiction, I think that the Minister of Justice might, on the occasion of some discussion with the various provincial attorneys general come to an agreement, so that, throughout the country, permits for the possession of firearms be delivered only in extreme cases, and that permits now valid which are given out to practically everybody, be cancelled, and thus heavily reduce the number of firearms in circulation today.

Supply-Justice
Moreover, I believe that the article in the Criminal Code regulating the carrying of arms should be amended. I know from experience that our police courts impose a minimum penalty on individuals found to be in possession of firearms without a permit. I submit that in such cases, we should amend the law so as to provide that anyone with a police record, and found in possession of a firearm, should be sentenced to prison without the alternative of a fine. Thus, we would, as I said, meet the wishes of our trial judges and of our police court magistrates.
Public opinion is aroused because today people carry weapons on the street, either with a permit or without one-which makes it even worse-because it is known that if you are caught, all you have to do is pay a few dollars, but there is no jail term. If public opinion demands that the law be made more strict in that respect-I think we should be guided by public opinion and should not ignore it-I would ask the Minister of Justice, who surely is aware of the problem, whether he expects to place before the house, in the near future, an amendment to the Criminal Code with a view to providing stiffer penalties in such cases. Moreover, I submit that the present penalty is not heavy enough, and that the situation should be looked into as soon as possible.
The Minister of Justice surely knows that on certain election days, hundreds of armed individuals walk our streets without permits.
This is a situation that must be brought to an end. When such abuse takes place, it is our duty to make the required changes in the legislation.
Therefore, I would ask the minister to tell us whether he intends to introduce amendments of this kind in the house, and if it is not his intention, I should like to know why.

I rise to bring to the attention of the minister the third and last matter that I have been asked to bring to his attention. This is a question that concerns three groups of people, namely those that are interested in civil rights and fundamental freedoms, those that are interested in the tourist trade and those that are interested in health and comfort as far as clothing is concerned.
My question is: What legal authority have civic authorities to make bylaws to determine the style or length of Canadians' clothing? I mention this because the body of opinion which is protesting the action of town coun-

cils and village councils is a substantial body of opinion in Canada. I want to make quite clear that I am raising this complaint as a member of parliament who has promised to bring it to the attention of the minister and as one who is quite neutral whether shorts should be two inches below the knees or two inches above.
There have been several articles in newspapers throughout Canada as well as letters in papers across this country, and I should like to quote an article from the Montreal Gazette of June 24 in which I see the question is of some concern to eastern townships. The article is entitled "Magog agog over 'short' rule", and I want to quote one or two paragraphs to indicate to the minister the concern over this matter, similar to the sort of concern which has been expressed in other places. The article says:
Visitors to this eastern township vacation centre are warned: The city fathers have passed what has been described as ai "shortsighted" bylaw.
If any female resident or tourist is seen wearing "short shorts" in the streets, she is liable to a severe lecture from a passing policeman. The definition of "short," according to the lawmakers, is shorter than two inches above the knees.
Then the article goes on to deal with the various penalties and concludes:
But the bylaw remains in effect and Police Chief Telesphore Lavoie's men have their orders. No tape measures have been issued to the constables, so they will have to make up their own minds.
The worst offenders? According to past police experience, they're the elderly visitors.
I have been asked to ask the minister these two questions. Under what legal authority are these bylaws passed by town councils and village councils and other civic authorities with respect to the length of clothing; and are they in transgression of civil rights and fundamental freedoms? People want to know whether they should direct their complaints to the provincial authorities or to the municipal or civic authorities in question. They want to know what basic right civic authorities have to determine the length of Canadian ladies' leg coverings.
I hope that when the minister replies his reply will contain the information that various people are seeking. They will know the facts so far as the legal position is concerned, and after the minister has given his answer they will know where to direct their representations, whether to the province or to the municipalities. Mind you, some persons may think this is a trivial matter, but it is of some concern to persons operating tourist resorts, persons who cater to tourists and that sort of thing in various parts of Canada

It is on behalf of these three groups particularly interested, namely those interested in civil rights and fundamental freedoms, those interested in the various industries and those interested in health and comfort, that I raise this matter this afternoon.

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased you recognized me directly following the hon. member for Kootenay West, because if you had not I intended getting the floor on a question of privilege. This is something Which I have some interest in, not from the point of view of the subject matter itself but because the hon. member for Kootenay West on another occasion dealt with a subject matter which came under the jurisdiction of the Department of Health and Welfare and referred to lipstick. He went on to mention that he was too old to engage in osculatory exercises and was not immediately concerned.
Unfortunately from my point of view, on that occasion a newspaper reporter, I think in one of the columns of an Ottawa newspaper, attributed that remark to me, that is to say the remark about osculatory exercises, and of course such was not the case for even in my wildest moments I would not make such a comment. However, in this case I hope that the same newspaper man or other newspaper men will not attribute those comments just made by the hon. member for Kootenay West to myself.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I deal with the matters raised in the order in which hon. members spoke.
The hon. member for Kootenay West raised the matter of dominion Q.C.'s and suggested, in effect, that the federal right to recommend the appointment of dominion Q.C.'s should be used to fill in gaps left in the provinces because of the fact that sometimes, as he put it-I did not make the charge-governments tend to appoint as Q.C.'s only those who are persona grata to that government.
I	am not going to enter into any particular defence or criticism of any provincial government, but while what the hon. member said may have some foundation in fact and perhaps be a subject of criticism of provincial governments, it is also a fact that a study of the situation shows that provincial governments, at least in recent years, while they have perhaps not been as broadminded in this field as the hon. member would like to see them, or perhaps even as I would like to see them, have nevertheless been in the habit of appointing as Q.C.'s members of political persuasions other than that of the government of the day.
79951-0-3541
Supply-Justice
I know that to be the case in British Columbia where I am happy to say they are now following a policy of a very limited number of appointments to Q.C. Indeed I think this is much to be encouraged because most members of the bar, when they think about the matter seriously, agree that to some extent Q.C.'s are handed out altogether too freely and frequently to members who are not really qualified. I do not mean they are not qualified politically but members of the bar who do not go into courts and whose work really is not opinion work, and that sort of thing. So I think British Columbia is following an admirable course in very severely restricting the number of
Q.C.'s which annually are appointed.
Is that the case in the province of Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is a matter which the hon. member might take up with the appropriate provincial authorities. I do not know what the situation is in other provinces but I had a quick chance to discuss it with members from New Brunswick and Ontario, and certainly in those provinces, and also I am told in others, the award is not confined to those of the political persuasion of the government of the day. 1 mention that because it is a reason why I should not appoint as dominion Q.C. persons who are simply not appointed by the provinces.
There is another and I think better reason, and that is that it is my view that the appointment of a dominion Q.C. should be confined to those persons whose work at the bar is of a nature where the dominion government has some proper interest in making the recommendation. That is, generally speaking, to persons in the civil service. Obviously in the past persons in the government itself have been recommended and received this appointment, and also perhaps members of boards and commissions constituted under the authority of the dominion parliament may be appointed.
I am very definitely of the view that appointment as dominion Q.C. should be confined to persons in those categories, and I think there is a very good reason for it. These persons would not normally be recommended for appointment by a provincial government because their work is not primarily in provincial courts or their service does not bring them to the attention of the provincial authorities. Therefore 1 think we should confine our appointments to those whose service is of a dominion or national nature or significance. I think it would be very dangerous for us to single out people in provinces who have not that sort of

Supply-Justice
qualification I have mentioned and make them dominion Q.C.'s. That of course, as the hon. member realizes, carries the precedence and honour in all the provinces of the country, whereas the appointment of a provincial Q.C. applies only to the province in which it is made. So I regret I cannot accept the hon. member's recommendation in that field.
Coming to his last remarks about the legislative authority under which municipalities make bylaws with regard to women's dress, I can go a certain distance but no further in giving an answer. I am, of course, bound by the principle that the Minister of Justice does not give legal opinions on the floor of the House of Commons, especially on matters that are not within the administrative responsibility of the dominion government or the jurisdiction of the federal parliament. Subject to that, I can say that the authority for the municipality to pass a bylaw would, of course, be found in the provincial statute which sets up the municipality within the province and defines the areas within which it has the power to pass bylaws. Thus I think the hon. member and those who have consulted him should examine the municipal act of the province and seek to obtain their answer by an advice or opinion with respect to that act and the particular bylaw in question.
I do not think I can go further than that for the reason I have given, and also for the good reason that I am not aware of the particular problem in that particular area that may or may not be created by the length of women's dresses or by the habits of the ladies of that area with respect to their dresses or to the height of the seams from the ground. The hon. gentleman will have a much better knowledge than I as to whether that represents a danger to the peace and welfare of that particular community. I have not that knowledge, and therefore I cannot express an opinion as to whether it is desirable, let alone legal, that the length of women's dresses and shorts should be regulated.
With regard to what was said by the hon. member for Essex West on section 170 of the Criminal Code, I appreciate very fully the position taken by the hon. member in this regard and his deep convictions on the subject. Indeed, he has discussed it with me on more than one occasion and on each occasion when we have discussed it I have felt that to him it is improper that this provision should remain on the statute books, for the reasons he gave this afternoon.
My hon. friend advanced two main reasons, I think. First of all, he said that the change in the statute which brought about the present

position was inadvertent and unintended. More than that, parliament was told at the time this change was made that the change was not, in fact, being made. Second, my hon. friend objects because persons who are not, as he puts it, actually gambling, may be convicted of being in a common gaming house. I regret that at least as the situation stands at the present time I am not able to recommend any change in the law.
I have pointed out to the hon. gentleman, and would like to point out to the committee, that this matter has been discussed with all the provincial attorneys general and that with one exception they have expressedly or by implication indicated that they were happy with the law as it now is and wanted it to remain that way. One area in which it has been indicated clearly that they would accept the change to the former position is the province of Ontario. In these circumstances I think it would be dangerous, if not improper for me to suggest amending the law as I am asked to do by the hon. member for Essex West. I think my position is that I must examine and take responsibility for the law as I found it when I assumed my appointment as Minister of Justice.
I think the position would have been different, and I would have been in a different and indeed, difficult position, had I been Minister of Justice at the time the change was made and had I given the assurance which was given then that no change was going to be made. I know

and I know also that the hon. member agrees with this-that the assurance which was given by the minister of justice at the time was made in good faith; it was only when the Supreme Court of Canada passed on the act that it was realized a change had been made. If I was in the position that I had given that assurance and then found that my assurance had not been correct and that, in fact, parliament had changed the law on my recommendation, I would be in a difficult position and I might then be under an obligation to recommend to parliament that the law should be changed back.
However, I am not in that position. I am assured by the majority of the provinces that this law as now passed enables them to do what they had on a number of occasions desired to do by provincial statute only to find that those statutes had been declared ultra vires. After consideration by the provincial attorneys general and by the commissioners on the uniformity of laws on at least two occasions, it has been the clear desire of the majority that there should be no change from the section as it presently stands. In considering whether or not I should recommend

a change in the law I have to consider the public interest, and in doing that I have to be guided to a considerable extent by the views of those responsible for enforcing the Criminal Code. In these circumstances, where all the provinces but one clearly want the law to remain as it is, I think it is my responsibility to accept their views, which I do, and I accordingly regret that I am not able to recommend a change.
If, however, on reconsideration, and in the light of the arguments made by the hon. member or of any other considerations which may occur to them, either the provincial attorneys general or their representatives at the conference should wish to examine the matter again and come to a different conclusion I should be fully prepared to give immediate consideration to any different recommendation which they might make.

Could I ask the minister a question? My information is that the act is not being enforced in all the provinces, including some where the attorneys general seem to want the act to remain as it is now. Will some inquiry be made as to whether this act is being enforced in all those provinces by the departments of the attorney general concerned and, if not, why not?
