speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask if there is any difference in the principles that are applied by the parole board as compared with the principles applied by the former remission service?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Not very great differences in the principles, Mr. Chairman, except that in the operation of the parole board we are endeavouring to avoid what used to be called a rule of thumb, namely that persons had to have served one half of their sentence before they were considered for parole. The Parole Act itself requires that the board review immediately the case of every person who enters the penitentiary and make an assessment of his or her situation with respect to the time at which a definitive review should be made with regard to parole, whether or not the man or woman has served half of his or her sentence.
In addition, the board is required to review the cases of all those who were presently serving penitentiary terms at the time the board began its operations. This review has been practically concluded, and will be concluded within a few weeks. Within those limits, the principles on which parole will be granted are, I am informed, much the same.
The present board has visited every penitentiary in Canada and interviewed a large number of inmates. The board has endeavoured to make it clear that the governing consideration on the basis of which parole will be granted is the attitude of the inmate; that there is no completely hard and fast rule. What the board wants to find out is whether the inmate's attitude toward his rehabilitation in society is constructive or otherwise; if he shows himself or she shows herself as being worthy of parole, then the board will consider that case for parole.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What is required by the board for the initiation of a case?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The terms of the act, as I say, require on commitment an immediate review of every file. Then the files must be reviewed within six months, and then they are reviewed again within a year and every two years thereafter. There is, therefore, an automatic process for bringing files forward for review

which commences immediately upon admittance of the inmate to the penitentiary.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Assuming there is a case where a person desires review within the two year period, how does he proceed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The inmate may submit an application form directly to the board requesting a review for parole.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: How does the board proceed once the case is before it? Are the files only reviewed or are witnesses heard by the board?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The penitentiary file is reviewed upon the basis of which committal was made. In addition, reviews are requested from the magistrate or judge who heard the case, from the welfare agency and in some cases from the John Howard or Elizabeth Fry society. A most complete review of that nature is conducted. The inmate is interviewed personally by the regional representative, but there is no rule that requires the hearing of witnesses.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If someone wants to be heard on behalf of an inmate, can he be heard by the board?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The act says that the board is not obliged to hear witnesses, but I am advised that the board hears everyone who applies and in no case have they refused to hear a witness who has applied to be heard on behalf of an inmate.
What jurisdiction or discretion has the minister apart from or above and beyond the board?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The minister has no discretion, Mr. Chairman. One of the important recommendations in this field of the Fauteux committee was that the discretion should be removed from the minister on the basis, as I recall the report, not that the minister had intervened or that politics had intervened, but that they might. The committee's recommendation was that there should be set up a national parole board which should have absolute and final authority to decide whether or not an inmate should be paroled. The act was passed on that basis and the authority of the board is final.

I have a question, but I must
admit it is a most difficult one for me to ask. If a person is on good behaviour, then the parole board can come in. In a case where the parole board cannot move in, can the minister say what the situation is with regard to his powers? I know of some cases which disturb me a great deal, I admit. Two persons were sentenced to the penitentiary for long periods and their behaviour has been

such that for years they have been kept in solitary confinement. I agree that this must be done because one is an absolutely uncontrollable sex pervert and the other is completely uncontrollable in connection with violence. In normal cases they might be allowed out on parole because of good behaviour, but they have to be kept in solitary confinement, and, as I say, I agree that this has to be done. Is there any basis at all- I do not know how to put it-on release for care or with some provision or do you as minister have to release them on the public?
I have put the question rather confusedly but this is a most important matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think there is a mixture here. There is a question here that involves both the matter of the expiration of the sentence and the question of release on parole before the sentence has expired. In a case such as those which the hon. member has mentioned, taking the matter of parole first, the parole board would examine the file and interview persons to establish whether or not there has been a change of attitude on the part of the inmate; in other words, to establish whether this inmate's attitude now is such that he indicates he would make a good adjustment if he were released before his sentence had been completed. Even in these cases, if there were sufficient evidence that the attitude of the inmate had changed so that it would be a proper case for parole and the board were satisfied that it was a proper case where the safety of society would not be prejudiced, they might grant parole even before the expiration of the sentence.
Let us be realistic, however. I am not suggesting that this would be a likely eventuality in the case of the two inmates to which the hon. member has referred; but it is possible that if they themselves showed a change in their attitude they would then be considered for parole.
The other aspect or element of the question relates to the matter of their release at the expiration of their sentences. Suppose an inmate were sentenced to a 20-year term. Even suppose that by his behaviour he had not earned any automatic time off for good behaviour, or that his behaviour had been bad, still at the end of the 20-year sentence there is no authority for his further detention and the penitentiary authorities would have no alternative but to release him because he had served the sentence which the court had imposed. Therefore unless his conduct in the penitentiary itself had made him subject to another criminal charge upon which he had been convicted and sentenced to an additional term-as I say unless that had happened-
Supply-Justice
he would have to be released at the end of the sentence for the offence for which the court had convicted him.

It is quite obvious that I have not got my point over yet, although I appreciate what the minister has said. The minister knows, as do all hon. members, of my interest in criminology and in getting men out on parole.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

I think this is the first time I have ever spoken in the House of Commons when I raised the question of individual cases. I am saying "two men" without naming them or the penitentiary. Under their terms of sentence, for years the warden has had to keep them completely in solitary, one because he is completely uncontrollable as a homosexual and the other because he is completely uncontrollable as to violence. As a matter of fact, he almost killed a guard. They have been in solitary all this time. Are these men insane? They must be insane. Otherwise why have they been kept completely segregated from everyone else for years? I am now asking the minister this question. When their penitentiary sentence is up are these two men I have in mind going to be turned out of the penitentiary when the experience over the years is that they are insane, uncontrollable, one a homosexual and one having a record of violence? Why have they been kept in solitary-and I know it for a fact-all these years and not being declared insane and put under the proper supervision? Owing to the fact that they have not been so dealt with, although they have been in solitary for these years I understand, from what the minister has now said as soon as their penitentiary term is over they can be released on society. That is the point I am after.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think the hon. member takes my answer a bit beyond the terms in which I gave it. What I said was that at the end of their sentence the penitentiary would have no authority to keep them in custody in the penitentiary any longer. I agree with the hon. member that it is not desirable to identify particular cases but I know perfectly well the cases of which he is speaking. In that connection all I can say is this. It is true that these particular inmates have been kept under the circumstances which he has outlined, in general for the reasons he has given. Under the terms of the Penitentiary Act, if an inmate is found to be suffering from mental disease or, in other words, is found to be insane we apply to have him committed to a provincial mental institution. There have been cases in which the provincial authorities have refused to accept

Supply-Justice
our finding that the man is insane, that he is a mental case rather than a penitentiary case. We have therefore kept those inmates during the period of their sentences and for the full extent of their sentences.
In a case such as that which is mentioned, all that could happen, and what would inevitably and undoubtedly happen, is that when the inmate reaches the end of his sentence a further examination of him will be held and subject of course to medical opinion at the time a finding as to his mental condition will be made; and, granted the circumstances which we have been discussing, my assumption is that he will again be certified as a mentally sick person or as an insane person. It will then be the responsibility of the provincial authorities to decide whether or not that finding is accepted and the inmate is committed to a mental institution or whether he should be released to society. But we will have no authority under which to detain him. Our recommendation will be clear but it will be the responsibility of the provincial authority to decide whether he is committed to a mental institution or released to society.
That is my very point. The Minister of Justice knows the cases that I am discussing.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

He knows that they have been kept in solitary now for a great length of time for the reasons I have outlined. Although they are in the penitentiary under charges and are admittedly insane, why is it that they have not been committed to an institution for the criminally insane?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We are now discussing the penitentiary administration very clearly. I would prefer to answer this question under the penitentiary items. I think I know the answer but I want to give factually and legally correct answers and, if my hon. friend does not mind, I would prefer to continue this discussion under the penitentiaries items.
I do not want these men released on the general public. .

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As far as parole is concerned, which is the item we are considering now, I think I am perfectly safe in saying that if they applied they would not be considered for parole unless they showed a change in attitude, and since it appears they have not done or are not likely to do so, they would not be seriously considered for parole.

There is one question I should like to ask the minister. It is with regard to the degree to which the parole board

remits sentences or extends parole. There has been a sort of unwritten rule that every inmate must serve at least half of his sentence and that parole is not considered until after that period has elapsed. It is my understanding that there is nothing in the regulations governing the parole board in this regard and that parole can be considered at any time the parole board believes the inmate is ready to take his place again in society. I wonder whether the minister might comment on that matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes; and at the same time I should like to deal with a question which was raised by the hon. member for Saskatoon at an earlier stage this afternoon. The regulations made under the Parole Act which came into effect recently-
On what date?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: Or his length of service?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have indicated already the occasions on which his case is reviewed and I have made it quite clear that there is no arbitrary rule of thumb that he must have served a certain portion of his sentence, although the hon. member will appreciate, as will all hon. members of the committee, that there must be some general principles to guide the board with respect to matters of this kind. But the reviews are made at the periods I have indicated.
The hon. member for Saskatoon asked about the steps which are being taken to, I think he used the phrase, educate the public as to the purposes and advantages of parole, and I would like to draw his attention to the activities of the board members which have been carried on since they assumed their functions on February 15 last year.
There have been 26 television and radio interviews, four magazine articles and numerous press releases. Members of the board also had 35 meetings with prison inmate committees and made 37 speeches to magistrates' associations, to after-care agencies, university students, service clubs, and general public meetings in Canada. That was up till December 31 of last year. Since January 1 of this year addresses have been made on 26 separate occasions. There have been 15 television appearances, ten radio talks and further numerous press releases. Certainly I would judge, on the basis of the press comments which I have seen, that the efforts of the board, guided by its chairman in this respect, have been very successful indeed in creating a public acceptance of the work and objectives of the board, and also a public acceptance of the results of that work which, as I pointed out earlier, have had the effect that there were last year 2,038 paroles 79951-0-355
Supply-Justice
granted; that there have been up to the present day, June 24 this year, 3,044 paroles granted and a total of only 214 paroles forfeited or revoked. That is a total rate of failure of 7 per cent, which compares extremely favourably with the record of experience in other countries.
When hon. members stop to think that that means there were 3,044 paroles granted less 214 failures, or in other words 2,830 inmates would otherwise still be incarcerated who are now out on parole and successfully observing the conditions of their parole, thus better enabled to return to society as useful and law abiding members thereof-that is 2,830 people now in society as the result of these paroles within one year-then I think the decision of the government supported by parliament to set up a national parole board under the national parole act has been entirely vindicated.
I thank the minister for that information.

Mr. Chairman, I was very interested in the question raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East and the minister's reply. The minister read from a red covered book. He did not say he was enunciating regulations because we have not yet got the date of the statute which might govern these matters. But I was interested as to what kind of unorthodoxy perhaps is practised by the board in exceptional cases, or do they have a standard practice, a principle, or whatever you call it, even apart from a regulation or a law?
I think that was the point the hon. member for Vancouver East was pursuing. In how many cases has the board ever deviated under a special circumstance, relating to an individual for whom special representations had been made, from orthodoxy, principle, law, or anything else? To what extent does it use discretion, humanity and other considerations with respect to an isolated individual? Or irrespective of regulations, irrespective of law, do they have some kind of a routine thing which says that under no circumstances have they ever reduced a sentence of a person lower than, say, 50 per cent of what was awarded by the court?
I think perhaps that is what the hon. member for Vancouver East was pursuing and this concerns me. I am concerned as to what humanity, what discretion, what personal judgment is used by this board in these matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think the extent to which the board exercises its prerogatives of discretion and mercy may be gathered from the

Supply-Justice
fact that in 1958, the last year before the board commenced its operations, the total number of paroles granted amounted to 974. Again I can only repeat that for the calendar year in which the board became operative the number granted was 2,038. I hope that will impress the hon. member as being a complete answer to the question the hon. member asked as to whether the board is exercising the authority and discretion vested in it.

I do not think the minister has completely answered my question or, perhaps, that which was in the mind of the hon. member for Vancouver South. We are, of course, all impressed by any statement of the minister as to the number of people which have been dealt with by the board. Our concern was, I think, with regard to the extent such cases might indicate that the discretion was courageously used, that it deviated from the pattern which might say for instance: no one is to be allowed to serve less than 50 per cent of their sentences. I was interested not so much in the total number of paroles granted but in the extent to which the board has shown some individual discretion. Has the board deviated from a standard pattern or is it the prisoner of a standard pattern?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The board is flexible, not rigid; the board is guided by the questions which it itself asks as to whether an inmate has shown by his attitude that he is ready for parole. However, the board is also guided by practical considerations-the good of society and the attitude and conduct of the inmate rather than any special compassionate feature. In other words, this board seeks to return to society on its own discretion and authority the greatest possible number of inmates who are ready to resume their places in society as constructive and useful members thereof.
These are the principles that guide the board. I have given the house figures to show that within these principles the board has been constructive and has rendered great service in the application of these principles to the cases that came before it. I am sure the hon. member would not expect me to go into details of individual cases nor do I intend to do so. What I have tried to do is to indicate, first of all statistically, the practical results of the board's operations, the encouraging results in terms of the low rate of failure, and then, in general to outline the policies by which the board is guided and which have brought about these satisfactory results.

I was more concerned about the percentage of paroles that might

have been granted by the board which involved reducing a sentence to below one third, or below one half rather than in statistics of the kind the minister has mentioned. I was thinking of evidence to show that the parole board really looks at individuals and takes initiative, showing what I might call guts in cases of this kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the hon. member could gather information of that kind from the figures I gave as to the number of applications denied and the number granted, but if he wants to assess the results on the basis of a comparison with the old half-time rule, I can give him these figures: of the number paroled, the percentage who served less than 35 per cent of their time was less than 2 per cent; the number who served between 35 per cent and 50 per cent was less than 13 per cent; the number who served between 50 per cent and 70 per cent was 67 per cent, and the number who served more than 70 per cent of their term was 18 per cent. So that the exceptions to the old half-time rule amount to 14.75 per cent.
I thank the minister. That was the answer I wanted.

I notice that the minister referred to inmates of penitentiaries when answering the hon. member for Laurier and that when he replied to the hon. member for Vancouver East he said cases were reviewed after 6 months, 12 months and 18 months. Are we to understand that the same rules apply in the case of inmates in common jails.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. The authority of the board under the act does not extend to the automatic review of the cases of inmates sentenced to terms in provincial jails. There has to be an application, and the rule the board has set itself is that these cases should be reviewed not later than four months of the time of receipt of the application.
Is the board considering terms of sentence less than six months in length?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. The case of any inmate sentenced to whatever term who submits an application for review is then reviewed.
Within four months?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, at the most.

I think this is one of the most interesting discussions on this subject we have had in the time I have been here, and I want to thank the minister and his aides for the information they have given. In view of what has been said about the success, or apparent success, of this system since the change was made; in view of the

number who have been released from parole and the comparatively small percentage who have had to go back because they broke the law, may I ask the minister whether he has any intention of initiating a policy whereby the judge or the jury continues to find a person guilty, but a body outside the court, such as we now have, will determine the length of sentence? I think the minister is familiar with the principle upon which I am asking him to comment, and I should like him to give us an indication whether he is moving in that direction. The judge or the jury cannot have all the reports and all the background which are so helpful and necessary if a man is to be justly sentenced.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I must say frankly that we do not contemplate such a system, certainly not at the present time. The hon. member will, I am sure, recall that the Fauteux committee did consider such a system but recommended against it. We do, however, have in mind taking all the steps we can to encourage judges, who have responsibility and will continue to have responsibility for sentencing, to visit institutions-and particularly when we have our new correctional reform program under way-in which sentences are served so that they may be-if I may put it this way without disrespect to the bench-better informed as to the type of training and rehabilitation program which is available for inmates and can determine the sentence, the length of sentence and perhaps the type of sentence, accordingly, on the basis of what this accused and guilty person needs. Does he need a long sentence to enable him to have a lengthy period of training reformation? Does he need only quick, exemplary punishment and quick results? Is that what he needs? Where is the institution where he can get what he needs? Therefore, what sentence should I impose accordingly?
This is a long term program and it will depend upon whether the judges are prepared to accept our invitation, which will be extended, to visit our institutions. I may say there are already some judges who take a personal as well as a judicial interest in the welfare and the history of persons whom they have sentenced and who do already follow up by visits to institutions. What we really hope to do is to extend that so that the sentence will come into the minds of the judges as a scientific and social matter. When I say "social" I mean in terms of what measure of reform, or training or rehabilitation or punishment the person before him requires.

Is it still the regulation and definite policy under the new system of 79951-0-3554
Supply-Justice
parole that a person must serve half a sentence? If the board believes that a person is rehabilitated does it have authority to release him on parole before half the sentence has been served?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman. Unequivocally, I say the board is not bound by any rule of thumb to half time.
That was the point of my question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I had answered it three times already.

I am sorry to be taking up so much time but I have one more point. What is the relationship now between the new change which came in last year and the remission services in the provinces? I am not supposed to mention names but I am going to. I have had something to do with a number of cases and I am very proud to see Mr. MacLeod before the minister. I have felt that in certain circumstances remission should have been granted but it was impossible because it did not come under federal jurisdiction; it came under provincial jurisdiction. What is the situation now under the new relationship? Just how far do the federal board's powers extend? I think the federal board is more sympathetic toward the parole system than some of the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The powers of the national parole board are set out in the Parole Act. The relationship between the national parole board and the provincial probation services is very good. The functions of the two are different and the authority is different. Probation services, as will be realized, are largely provincial and they relate to persons who may not be sentenced. A judge may put a man out on probation. We do not have any extensive probation services under the federal authority. These are provincial. They are officers of the court; but the parole board makes extensive use of the information, the knowledge and the skills of provincial probation services and their officers in obtaining assessments, reports and recommendations as to cases which come before our board for parole. The relationship between the two is very close. If we let a man out on parole we may in turn ask a provincial probation officer to be the supervisory officer with respect to that inmate's parole. In every way the relationship is very close but the statutory authority of the two, the parole board on the one hand and the provincial probation service on the other, is, of course, governed by the respective statutes under which they operate.

Supply-Justice
Does the parole system apply to persons who have been sentenced to jail for fewer than three years?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I beg your pardon, I did not catch the question.
Does the parole system which is operated under federal legislation apply to provincial jails? I do not think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The national parole board has jurisdiction over all persons who are serving sentences under the Criminal Code, whether they are serving those sentences in a federal penitentiary or in a provincial jail. They have that jurisdiction with respect to parole; they do not have jurisdiction with respect to persons who are serving sentences in provincial jails for offences against provincial statutes.
In addition, in Ontario and British Columbia there are provincial parole boards which do have jurisdiction over persons who are serving indeterminate sentences in provincial jails. The provincial parole board has jurisdiction over those.

That is one of the very points I had in mind. I am grateful to the minister for that answer. I think he will agree with me that this has caused a great deal of confusion. There is a conflict there in that the federal parole board has jurisdiction over those who are serving sentences in provincial jails if the sentence is one day under two years and if they have been convicted of a charge under the Criminal Code. If it is a charge under the provincial act, although the sentence may be exactly the same, the federal parole system cannot operate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is correct.

To my way of thinking this has caused a great deal of confusion in the past. As the minister knows, I have tried to handle a great number of cases, and sometimes I have been able to operate with success and in other times I have not. I have consulted with wardens-I am speaking now of the present situation-and I have been told at times that it did not come under our jurisdiction. Is this not a matter that should be clarified? Should not the matter of jurisdiction be made clear? I have always received complete co-operation and have been successful at the federal level, but I have not yet got an answer to a letter from the provincial parole board.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I agree with the hon. member that there is here a separation of jurisdiction that I think follows necessarily from the provision of the constitution under which Canada operates.

The Fauteux commission made certain recommendations in this field with respect to certain changes which the provinces might make in the jurisdiction and operation of their boards. But, of course, we are not in any position to dictate what they should do. All I can say, therefore, is that there are limitations on our authority and jurisdiction and there are areas in which the provinces are entitled to operate under their own exclusive authority and jurisdiction. We are endeavouring, both at the departmental level and through direct contacts between the board and its officers and provincial parole and probation boards, to work out a satisfactory method of co-operation so as to avoid overlapping and particularly so as to avoid differences in policy and differences in approach to these problems.
Provincial jails are completely under provincial jurisdiction but if inmates are sentenced under the Criminal Code then the federal government does have jurisdiction with respect to parole?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is quite clear. The operation of the jail and the circumstances and conditions under which inmates serve their sentences in the jail, if it is a provincial jail, are, of course, within the authority of the provincial legislature and officials, but that relates to the operation of the jail. The authority of the parole board does not extend to the conditions under which a man will serve his sentence in a jail. Their authority only extends to the question of whether he shall be paroled before he has served his sentence. Our board does not have authority and does not attempt to assert any authority as to the conditions under which a man will serve his sentence while he is in the provincial jail. All they say is whether or not he should be released from custody prior to the expiration of his sentence, which is an entirely separate jurisdiction from that of actually running the institution itself.

I am sorry, but I want to get it clear. The federal parole board has jurisdiction with respect to parole in the case of a person sentenced under the Criminal Code but has no jurisdiction if he is sentenced under an act of the legislature?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is correct.
How does that differentiation come about? It is a matter of parole, not administration of the jail.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It comes about because under the constitution we have no jurisdiction to set up a parole board with authority over sentences which are imposed by courts under provincial statutes. Our authority in this

field is confined to the Criminal Code which by the constitution is entrusted to the federal parliament, and since we have the authority to make criminal law we also have the authority to set up a parole board or the authority to parole persons who are convicted of criminal offences. But we have no authority to parole persons who are convicted of offences against provincial statutes and who are serving their sentences in provincial jails.

Mr. Chairman, following the interpretation just given by the Minister of Justice, which is probably right although it is a surprise to me, would it be possible to have the number of requests to the parole board for the parole of any inmate at the Bordeaux jail in Montreal in the past year?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If I were asked a general question as to the number of files we have reviewed I could, I suppose, give an answer in total, but to ascertain how many applications for parole have been received from a particular prison would entail a review of a vast number of files. If I were asked a question with respect to a particular inmate and asked how many representations were made on his behalf, we might be able to isolate it but I would hesitate to give such an answer on the floor of the House of Commons.
If the minister will permit me, I will be satisfied if he can tell me that the parole board has received one request in the past year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am given these figures for what is described here as the Montreal jail, which is Bordeaux. We denied 95 applications and granted 112.

Item agreed to.
159. Bankruptcy Act administration, $55,780.

Mr. Chairman, some remarks were made this afternoon with respect to the administration of the Bankruptcy Act by the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere and I should like to make a few additional remarks with respect to this legislation. It has come to my knowledge that debtors may go from one place in a province to another place in the same province in order to make an assignment. For instance, a man from Gaspe may go to Montreal to make an assignment in the hands of a trustee. If I am right, each province constitutes a district and within a province the chief justice may make several divisions. Again if I am right, the act is not obligatory so that a debtor is obliged to make an assignment in his division. He may go to another division.
Supply-Justice
Since there possibly will be a new codification of the act I should like the government to introduce an amendment to provide that a debtor will be obliged to make the assignment in his division so that creditors will not have to go from one part of a province to another in order to look after their interests. As the situation is now, a debtor from Gaspe may make an assignment in Hull and if all the creditors are from Gaspe they and the inspectors have to travel a long distance to meetings. It may be that the act is not administered well in the several divisions but in any event I should like this matter to be cleared up by the introduction of a specific provision in the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the point raised by the hon. member is one of those that we must take into careful consideration in the course of the review of the act that we will be making. I am told that at the moment the interpretation of the locality of a debtor, which means the principal place where the debtor has carried on business during the year immediately preceding his bankruptcy, etc., is a decision to be made by the official receiver in the case of an assignment. It may be that the act is not clear enough or that the safeguards against the practice to which my hon. friend has referred are not sufficient. That is one of the questions that we shall be looking at when we review the act because one of the things we are concerned about is whether the provisions of the act are sufficiently careful in their protection of the creditor or whether possibly they are not too lenient in the sense of looking after the debtor. That is one of the things we have to look at.

Mr. Chairman, since the minister has indicated that a review is to be made of the Bankruptcy Act there is one point I should like to draw to his attention for consideration. Following the decision of the supreme court to disallow bill No. 45 of the province of Alberta in 1959, which was a bill to provide for the orderly payment of debts and the consolidation of judgments and other debts and was patterned on legislation in force in Manitoba for 25 years and in Ontario for some 10 years, there now exists a certain void in the handling of debts for people who are really of very limited means. They are not corporations. Previously they had been dealt with in the province of Alberta by the debtors' assistance board. But this procedure is entirely voluntary. Unfortunately it has become the practice that certain creditors will attend a meeting where a debtor makes a composition or voluntary

Supply-Justice
proposal. Then one of the creditors will find out where this man is working and garnishee his wages.
Under the Alberta legislation, for example, a married man is exempt from garnishee up to $120 per month. However, by becoming completely destitute and going on relief, a man can receive sums ranging from $130 to $150 per month and so is better off than he is under his statutory exemption. There are, unfortunately, large numbers of men who are driven to this procedure because they are being hounded by their creditors. I would suggest to the minister that consideration should be given, under the summary administration provisions, on application by a province under section 5, subsection 1 of the act, that a debtors' assistance board or some public board or commission be authorized to act as trustee for summary administration of these very small estates.
I think hon. members will realize that under the normal procedures of bankruptcy a trustee cannot work for nothing, and unless there is something in the estate he is somewhat reluctant to accept the estate. In addition, these small estates entail a good deal of administration and, frankly, for what there is in it it is not worth while for the trustee to take on these matters. These debtors' assistance boards, if you want to call them that, could be appointed trustees to handle summary administrations only, with a view to formulating proposals rather than simply discharging the estate. They could do all the work by reason of the fact they are paid by the provincial authorities.
My point is simply that through the provision of the summary administration section of the act relief can be given to the small salaried worker who is in difficulty with his creditors.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I appreciate the comments of the hon. member, and I am aware of the difficulties created in Alberta as a result of the supreme court decision. Beyond saying what I have said about that, I would not like to comment. I am aware of the difficulties, and one of the particular features of the Bankruptcy Act which will come under review will be this part of it which provides for summary administration. We are concerned about that section and some of the abuses to which I think it is open at the moment. The intention is good, but there are some abuses to which it seems to be exposed, and although I would not care to comment as to what direction we will make changes, if and when we make changes, certainly the point that my hon. friend has in mind will be one that will be under review.

Item agreed to.

Penitentiaries-
161. Administration of the office of the commissioner of penitentiaries including $90,000 for grants to recognized prisoners' aid societies, as may be approved by the treasury board, $641,516.

I should like to ask the minister a question on item 161. Reference is made to $90,000 for recognized prisoners' aid societies as may be approved by the treasury board. I wonder if the minister would be kind enough to set out the criteria upon which the treasury board makes an examination of these applications for aid to the different societies?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It would be difficult for me to answer for the treasury board because the members of the treasury board alone could properly answer that. What I can answer for are the criteria which we observe in making our recommendations to the treasury board for what will be included in our estimates.
As the hon. member will appreciate, there are two headings under which we make grants to prisoners' aid societies or aftercare agencies, as they are variously called, that is under the national parole board, formerly the remission service, under which the sum of $60,000 is provided this year, and under the penitentiaries branch for which $90,000 is provided this year, making a total of $150,000.
The measure of the assistance they receive is, generally speaking, the number of cases in which they undertook assistance. The parole board calls upon them for assistance with respect to persons who are out on parole, and then they make a calculation of the number of cases in which this supervision or assistance has been given. The assistance to be given during the current year is based on the experience of the past year.
In the same way, under the penitentiary authority when a man is approaching his discharge date notification may be given to one of the agencies which would be asked to come in and interview the inmate, and do what they can to assist him after his discharge with respect to finding a job or in connection with the other problems with which he will be confronted. Again, the number of cases thus handled by the agency is kept, tabulated and the grant for the following year is based in general on the record of assistance in the preceding year.

I thought the minister had indicated earlier that he would have an extensive submission or statement to make under this item with respect to penitentiaries. Perhaps we could start the item off with that statement by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend is quite right. I am sorry, but possibly we made such progress that I did not keep up with the items. I did intend, and do intend, to make a statement on the progress to date in connection with our correctional and reform program, what has been done up to the moment, and a brief outline of what is planned for the future.
The various committees and other groups that over the years have made recommendations for improvement of the federal correctional system have invariably stressed the need for positive efforts to reform the offender through appropriate treatment and training in penal institutions and on parole. Since confederation the penitentiary system has usually lacked emphasis on reformative treatment. Some efforts in this latter direction have been made since world war II but they have been largely frustrated by continuing overcrowding in federal penitentiaries, lack of employment for inmates, an atmosphere of tension in the institution and, until last year, a lack of emphasis on parole as a rehabilitative measure for offenders.
As hon. members are aware, the responsibility of the government of Canada in so far as the operation of a prison system is concerned is to provide custody and reformative treatment for all persons who are sentenced under federal laws to imprisonment for two years or more. In 1952 the federal penitentiary inmate population was about 4,600. In the eight years since that time the inmate population has increased to over 6,300, an increase of almost 40 per cent. It is sobering to reflect that during that short period the number of young inmates-those under 21 years of age-increased from just short of 500 to slightly more than 900, an increase of about 80 per cent. In 1952 about 1,800 inmates were serving their second or subsequent penitentiary sentence. That number has now risen to about 3,000, an increase of 35 per cent or more.
These figures would seem to indicate that there is an increase in crime-at least in serious crime-in Canada and that the traditional methods of dealing with offenders by locking them up in prison and forgetting about them does not aid in solving the problem. Ninety-nine per cent of persons who are sentenced to penitentiaries sooner or later return to the community. Indeed over the last ten years some 23,000 inmates of federal penitentiaries have been released from custody, and their numbers alone indicate the necessity of ensuring that the prison experience should have a reformative effect upon the prisoner. Only thus can the public be protected when he is again at large.
Supply-Justice
Over the last year and a half the Department of Justice has made a substantial effort in the direction of reducing overcrowding in federal penitentiaries and also in providing more effective training for inmates confined in the penitentiaries. A new medium security institution designed to hold 450 inmates has been opened at Kingston, Ontario. A similar type of prison called the Leclerc Institution will be opened at St. Vincent de Paul near Montreal toward the end of this year.
A minimum security institution-that is a prison without walls, bars or guns-has been opened at William Head near Victoria, British Columbia. Another one has been opened at Valleyfield, Quebec and a third will be opened within a few months at Springhill, Nova Scotia. Each of these institutions is an example of the economical use of existing governmental facilities that can be adapted for prison purposes. The William Head installation was a Department of National Health and Welfare quarantine hospital that was surplus to the department's requirements. The Valleyfield installation was originally a small military camp. The Springhill institution has been developed for the most part by using available huts that were acquired from the Department of National Defence.
The result of these developments during the past year and a half is that whereas formerly federal penitentiary facilities consisted of maximum security institutions only, there are now to be found in the system examples of medium security institutions and minimum security institutions. In addition the department is now proceeding with plans for the development of correctional work camps. These will be camps for the custody, treatment and training of penitentiary inmates for whom maximum or medium security conditions of confinement are not necessary or appropriate. They will be designed to carry out improvement programs upon dominion or provincial crown lands such as the development of public parking areas or picnic grounds, reforestation programs, forest fire prevention programs, restoration of historical sites and reclamation of unused lands. The projects will be of a type that the governments concerned are not prepared to undertake with privately employed labour for say a period of approximately 10 years. Initially we would hope that this new type of camp, which will provide work and steady employment for about 75 inmates in each case, would be located in the provinces of Quebec, Ontario, Saskatchewan and British Columbia. Exploratory conversations are now being carried on in the province of Manitoba.

Supply-Justice
The development of these camps will enable the department to avoid the heavy expenditures by way of capital and maintenance costs that are involved in building maximum or medium security institutions and also the delay that is involved in planning and building institutions of that type.
Another significant development during the past year and a half has been the coming into force of the new Parole Act and the commencement of operations of the new parole board. We had a discussion on this matter on the item under which the parole board estimate is contained and therefore I think I need do no more than remind the committee that the work of the parole board is an essential part of the over-all approach to the new correctional program.
There have also been developments in connection with the problem of narcotic drug addiction which also were discussed in detail and at some length on an earlier occasion. I will therefore do no more here than mention them and ask the committee to keep it in proper perspective in assessing the full extent of the correctional program which we have envisaged and upon which we are embarking.
In addition to the review I have just made of what has been done with respect to new types of institutions and the new approach in the field of parole and narcotics we have also been concerned to make changes within existing institutions. Here, as I have said, we are confronted with the problem created by overcrowding and the difficulties which that situation imposes upon us with respect to instituting or maintaining in those institutions proper work programs, rehabilitation programs, vocational training and other programs for the inmates that are there. I am quite sure that hon. members will realize without my enlarging upon it the difficulty with which we are confronted when space which should be used and is essential if you are going to carry out a proper training program has instead to be devoted to the mere physical accommodation of the number of inmates that we have because of this overcrowding situation.
Notwithstanding the difficulties that overcrowding has caused in penitentiaries it has been possible, in the existing maximum security institutions, to introduce certain improvements in the fields of classification and segregation and to expand the types of vocational and other reformative training for inmates. For example, new dormitories have been established outside the wall of St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary for 225 inmates. This action permits the segregation of this group of offenders from more hardened 
criminal elements who must be kept in custody behind the wall. It has been possible in Kingston penitentiary, which has a population of some 950 inmates, to provide accommodation and suitable reception and classification procedures for 50 inmates on a continuing basis. Similar reception facilities have been established at Saskatchewan penitentiary. At Manitoba penitentiary dormitory facilities have been established outside the wall to provide pre-release training for selected inmates who are approaching their day of discharge from custody.
New types of vocational training which involves the use of classroom techniques and on the job training, where the inmate learns a trade or occupation by actually working at it, have been introduced at most federal institutions. For example, training in electronics is now given at the federal training centre in Quebec and at British Columbia penitentiary. At several institutions new training courses in the welding and sheet metal trades have been started and the number of inmates receiving training in such trades as plumbing, carpentry and masonry has been increased. A commercial class in typing, shorthand and bookkeeping has been started at Dorchester penitentiary.
With regard to these work programs generally may I say that one of our programs has been to provide a useful day's work for an inmate so that he would have a feeling of self-respect, a feeling that he was doing something in which he could take some pride and also so that he might be accustomed or acclimatized, if you wifi, to the conditions which he would have to meet when he leaves the institution where he will be expected to do a full day's work for a full day's pay.
With this overcrowding condition with which we have been faced, with the concurrent problems I have outlined, we have found that the traditional prison day for a penitentiary inmate up to the present has generally found him locked in his cell before five o'clock in the afternoon and not released again until seven o'clock the following morning. It would seem that such an extended period of closed custody for an inmate every day, without an opportunity to associate with other human beings or to receive the benefit of training and counselling from staff members, is not calculated to prepare an inmate for the many problems that he has to face upon his return to free society.
Accordingly for the past half year an experiment has been conducted at Kingston penitentiary whereby substantial numbers of inmates, sometimes numbering as many as 200 or 250, are released from their cells during the early evening hours for educational

and recreational purposes. These inmates play organized sports in the auditorium, watch educational movies and television programs or browse in the prison library. Thus far this experiment has demonstrated that it aids in the socialization of the inmate who in so many respects must live such an unnatural type of life in the institution and greatly promotes the lessening of tension which, if permitted to build up unduly, tends to lead to disturbances in the institution. It is certainly to be hoped that this form of evening training can be extended to other penitentiaries.
A program designed to help the inmate become aware of his responsibilities to the free community when he is released and also to help him achieve a better understanding of himself and his fundamental problems is carried on at Collin's Bay penitentiary in Ontario and also at British Columbia penitentiary. This program is proving to be successful and the intention is to extend it to all institutions.
In concluding my remarks in connection with this brief review of plans for the future and progress to date, I want to emphasize one thing, and that is that while my emphasis is, and I think must properly be, upon the changes we expect to make for the future, I would not want it to be overlooked that although we stress the shortcomings and the changes which should be made and ask parliament to support us in this expenditure we are asking for in order to make those changes, nevertheless credit must be given and never overlooked to the penitentiaries staff which have carried on so admirably in the past under the limited and difficult circumstances with which they have been faced. I think it is to the credit of the Canadian penitentiary system that our institutions have been run so free of trouble and by and large have done what could be done to turn an inmate out a better man than when he went in, and it has done that notwithstanding the limited resources with which it has had to work.
So I hope that the committee, in turning its face to the future and supporting us with respect to our program for the future, will not allow its concentration on future reforms -challenging and stimulating as they are- will not allow that emphasis on that aspect to overshadow altogether the debt of gratitude we owe to the staff who have served very faithfully in the past and at present.

Mr. Chairman, I have no doubt that the program outlined by the minister is already bringing good results, but what worries me is what happens when an inmate gets his freedom.
As the minister knows, because of the present situation with regard to unemployment it is very hard for a man who gets his
Supply-Justice
freedom and enters civil life to find work. In this connection I should like to know whether we are making any efforts in this respect. Have we got rehabilitation officers assisting the inmate who has just got his freedom to find work? To what extent are we successful in this regard?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is a special placement section in the national employment service which, on notification that an inmate is within three months of his discharge date, sends a representative to interview him in the institution in order to analyse his past record of employment, assess his capabilities, and then the official returns and tries to find a job opportunity for him upon the inmate's discharge.
In addition to that, our parole officers across the country are available to serve not only inmates on parole but discharged inmates who may have problems in connection with employment. I should of course pay special tribute here to the work done by the voluntary after-care agencies such as the John Howard and Elizabeth Fry societies which do tremendous work in obtaining employment opportunities for inmates.
Although it will take a long time to develop, I am sure, we have in mind for the future an individual sponsorship program through the agencies of the voluntary organizations as well as through our own staff with the objective-this is an objective only; I am not giving a blueprint-that ultimately it might be possible for individual inmates to be sponsored by individuals or organizations even before they leave the penitentiary with a view to personal assistance in replacing them in society and particularly in placing them in jobs. We cannot place the onus exclusively on the individual or voluntary agency; we must accept a large part of the responsibility ourselves as the penitentiary branch, the parole service, and so on, but the objective is that every inmate who requires help in finding employment opportunities will receive personal assistance in doing so.

I should like to bring a couple of minor points to the attention of the minister. I spent a day with Warden Cummins in Westminster and I must say Mr. Cummins is one of the finest men I have ever met and I believe he must be of very great assistance to the department. But there are several rules which seem to be necessarily restrictive. For instance, when writing letters a prisoner is allowed one sheet of paper and he is limited to how many letters he can write. One particular prisoner wrote on both sides and wrote so finely that they said, "You can have two or three sheets of paper to write letters on".

Supply-Justice
Another point is with regard to visitors. This warden told me the regulations say that particularly female visitors have to be women of good repute and relatives; so he has more aunts of prisoners than really the prisoners have. As they say, they have to come in under the guise of being a relative. These prisoners need that contact with the outside world. He told me the story of one prisoner who said, "Warden, you know the sort of man I am and the life I have led; what decent self-respecting woman do you think would ever associate with me?"
In this effort of rehabilitation I think of these two considerations. I would think the penitentiary officials would want these men to do all the writing they possibly could. I was there last fall and maybe the regulations have been changed since then, but if they have not they certainly should be changed. In regard to visitors there should be a certain amount of reason exercised. I think there may be other regulations which have the same effect, but these two particular regulations I am talking about certainly are not conducive to helping a man keep in touch with the outside world and keeping him semi-prepared anyway for his re-entry into outside life.
As I said, I spent a day out there. I thought the penitentiary was exceedingly well run; the food was good. I do not suppose you could say the inmates looked happy, but they certainly looked contented, and I would like to pay tribute to Warden Cummins and the staff of British Columbia penitentiary.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to support what has just been said by previous speakers. I know that we cannot under any circumstances mollycoddle those who have broken the law. If they break the law they have to accept the punishment for it. But I feel that the view of the Minister of Justice is that although there must be punishment and retribution, if you want to put it that way, the main aspect of the question is rehabilitation.
When one enters a penitentiary he goes into an entirely different world. I think it is about four weeks that you are in one section of the prison where you are questioned, where you are told the rules, where they try to understand you and then decide what you should do. After that, you are committed to the prison routine.
As I said this afternoon, I cannot understand a man wanting to go back to a life of that kind. Nor can I understand how a man can be placed in a position to rehabilitate himself when he is strictly limited in his contacts with the outside world. I agree with those who have said that there should be

humanity with discipline and with punishment. To cut a person off from contact with those he knows and loves in the outside world is bad. Few things could be worse than the suppression of facilities for writing and receiving letters. Every letter, both in and out, is censored, so that the prison authorities know exactly what both the man and his correspondents are writing. Surely it is a good' idea to keep these persons in contact with those they love and trust.
Mr. Chairman-or I should say, Madam Chairman. I am sorry; I was so interested in talking that I did not notice who had taken the chair-I believe the increase of these contacts is good, first because it helps toward rehabilitation and increases contact with the outside world and, second, because it provides a far better method of discipline than reliance on restriction and corporal punishment.
I am opposed to corporal punishment. I am opposed to severe discipline. I agree there has to be discipline, but this I know from years of visiting jails and penitentiaries; I have not met more than three inmates who would not prefer to take the lash or the paddle than to lose the privileges which they receive, whether they take the form of cigarettes, or reading matter, or radio, or the writing and receiving of letters. It is in the control over these privileges that the penitentiary authorities have the greatest power. That is the way in which the authorities can exercise discipline, by cutting out visitors and by cutting out the writing and the receiving of letters. I was very proud that one of my colleagues spoke earlier on this subject. I want to support what he said and ask that greater consideration be given to this phase of our subject.
There is one other matter that I wish to discuss, and the minister may perhaps be somewhat amazed that I should raise the question at the moment. The hon. gentleman spoke about the training which takes place at penitentiaries, training in masonry, carpentry and so forth. I know that in British Columbia at the present time we have a very serious unemployment problem, and there may be some who will misunderstand the proposal I am about to make. Over the years I have read with a great deal of interest what is being done in some of the states in the United States and what is being done in other countries in Europe where the authorities in charge of prisoners have sought to obtain the co-operation of employers and trade unions in this training work. I should like to ask the minister whether any approach along these lines has ever been made through the trade unions of Canada. I should like to know whether the trade unions have ever been asked to interest themselves in this

problem of the rehabilitation of those who have broken the law. Have we ever asked the unions to co-operate and send into the institutions their experts in the fields of electronics, inside and outside wiring, carpentry, plumbing and so on as part of the educational process? It may be that when the inmates are released after completing their sentences they could continue in the work which they have learned as apprentices, improvers or journeymen. A certain number might be accepted in the trade union of the particular craft they have chosen and be sponsored by that particular trade union which would assist in their efforts to become rehabilitated.
I have read that in countries where this has been attempted it has proved very successful, and that co-operation between the trade unions, the employers and the prison authorities has worked out extremely well. I should like to ask the minister whether this approach has ever been tried in Canada and whether he thinks this is worth attempting.
I raise this question now at a time when a great many trade unionists are themselves out of work, but I am speaking on the principle, and I believe it would be well worth while to approach employers and trade unions on this matter of helping to instruct the inmates of our penitentiaries by means of lectures and so on and then invite them to co-operate to an extent as the prisoners come out and try to rehabilitate themselves. I think such an effort would be well worth while.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: To deal with the last mentioned subject first, I can assure the hon. member that we have had over the years extensive contacts and consultations with trade union organizations. I think particularly of Collin's Bay where trade union representatives came down and assisted us in setting up the training programs. They also attended the training graduation ceremonies of the inmates and took part in those celebrations. I am told they also donated a number of prizes for efficiency in the training programs that were carried on. We have close contacts with trade union organizations. I am not saying it could not be improved; probably indeed it could, as we bring more and more moves to bear and have more and more facilities for programs of vocational training. But we do have close relations with the trade union organizations.
Can the minister tell me of one trade union sponsored individual? I want it carried on.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I cannot give the name at the moment but I am advised that certain trade
Supply-Justice
unions have arranged for examinations of our inmates who have had their vocational training courses, and as a result of that examination they are given credit for their journeyman certificates which they complete when they go outside. That arrangement is not an unusual one to be made with respect to inmates and with respect to the relations with trade unions.
My hon. friend asked me about the contacts with the outside world. I am informed there are numerous channels of contact with the outside world for our inmates. There are, for instance, such associations as Alcoholics Anonymous for one. I am told that in some instances there are meetings of as large a number as 50 to 75 which take place through that organization. There are many other group visits and group discussions which are arranged between inmates and outside organizations.
In regard to mailing privileges, I can only say that the penitentiary regulations generally are being reviewed. But when my hon. friend refers to British Columbia he must realize that at the moment there we are running a maximum security institution, a non-segregated institution, where unfortunately we do have to apply the maximum security regulations with regard to censorship and so on. We do have some staff limitations, and it is those conditions that necessitate that institution having quite severe restrictions with regard to mailing privileges; but they do not necessarily have to be applied in other institutions across the country. The regulations are being reviewed to see whether and to what extent relaxation can be allowed.

When the minister was making his remarks I thought he would give us some indication with respect to the minimum security personnel at Joyceville, which has a population of 450. I did not get the name of the other institution to which the minister made reference.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: l'lnstitut Leclerc.
This is in the offing; this is something for the future?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No; it will be opened this fall; construction is practically completed now.
Is it different from Joyceville?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is of the same general design as Joyceville; it will house approximately 450.

Can the minister give us some information on William Head, Valleyfield and Springhill?

Supply-Justice

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: William Head, 100; Valley-field, 100; Springhill, approximately 100.

Eleven hundred or 1,200,
something of that nature?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think 1,200.
With respect to William Head, is it not possible to establish additional facilities there to take in more inmates? I understand this can be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Of course, physically, we
could expand; probably we could increase the number of inmates but I think we would have to look very carefully at whether it is desirable in a minimum security institution to have many more than 100 inmates because you might destroy the atmosphere. There is a limitation on the number you can have without increasing your staff, and perhaps we would increase the staff more than one would want to. We are trying to establish an atmosphere almost next door to discharge. It is a progression that the inmates make and I question whether any more than 100 would be desirable in that type of institution.

Very well. The rough estimate which was given by the minister earlier was to the effect that in 1952 we had an inmate population of 4,600. As I recall it, this was very close to the total number of available cells in the institutions at that time, so that probably in 1952 or 1953 we were close to having the penitentiaries completely filled, if not to some degree overcrowded. Since that time up to today we have added another 1,700 to the present penitentiaries, not counting the Joyceville institution and the other ones. Conditions are such today that even when you get such places as William Head, Valleyfield and Springhill into operation fully and completely you will be no better off than you were eight or 10 years ago. We will still not be able to tackle the question of rehabilitation and reformation to any extent within the institutions themselves.
We need a much more expanded and accelerated program, and additional institutions must be opened. In addition to the number in our penitentiaries there are 1,000 inmates who are convicted under the narcotics act. As I understood the minister, he said at any one time about one third the total number of addicts were being processed through the institutions. We need additional institutions to deal with the narcotic addicts and perhaps this would remove some of the overcrowding; but this is something for the future. It is not something that is going to occur tomorrow. As the minister said, there are certain limitations on the funds available, and so on.
In all probability, if the trends of the past are any indication of the future, with an

increasing population in Canada, there is a possibility that we will continue to be in somewhat the same static position. The increasing facilities will not take care of the larger inmate population so that these institutions will be kept filled to the limit unless we can work effectively within the institutions on a program of reformation and rehabilitation.
I do not think it is possible to do this under the present program regardless of the highmindedness of the people interested in this country. I asked the minister a number of questions about this last session and he was kind enough to give me a great deal of statistical information which appears on page 4984 of Hansard of June 19 of last year. I should like to make reference to this overcrowding in so far as it affects shop space or other space that is used within the institutions themselves for sleeping purposes.
The minister indicated here that shop space and corridors were being used for dormitory purposes in some institutions. I am sure the hon. member for Vancouver South noticed that in the institution that he visited some time ago. In Kingston shops that could be used for training and everything else are now used for dormitories. In Dorchester, for instance, in shop space and corridors there were facilities for 13 inmates. In St. Vincent de Paul there were temporary dormitories either in shop space or corridors for 122; in Kingston, 184; in Saskatchewan, 60; in British Columbia, 94; and at Collin's Bay, 80. Incidentally, Collin's Bay is not a penitentiary in the old maximum security sense; it is a training centre: there are shops there, and even in the Collin's Bay penitentiary they have shop space and corridors taken up for inmates. This is indicative of the overcrowding which existed last year, and this is going to continue and continue. Will you call it ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman?

speechtext: May we deal first with the arrangement for Monday so that it will be definite? As I understand the proposal which hon. members are prepared to accept, it is that a supply motion will be moved on Monday but not debated.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is that agreed?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is so ordered.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Could we then have a decision with respect to the hours of sitting tomorrow, Dominion day?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is the house prepared to order that tomorrow's sitting be adjourned at one o'clock?

Business of the House
Agreed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is so ordered.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
With respect to the business for the other days of next week, Tuesday will be available for continuation of the debate on the bill of rights if so desired. If that should be completed, we have the department of forestry item on the order paper and there may be one or two other legislative
items which will appear by that time. Wednesday, Thursday and Friday will be given over to the discussion of estimates in the following order: completion of the Department of Justice and the R.C.M.P., national revenue, transport, external affairs, northern affairs, labour and public works.
It being ten minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
The following answer, deposited with the Clerk of the house, is printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:
